about: Anoria: 150 more cards from real history, found only in packs (a draft for Tim to read; nothing in the game loads this file yet): 100 Figures, 20 Relics and 30 Deeds. cards: one object per card, with the fields of cards.js (key, n, t, f, c, m, reg, era, y, k, arr, insp, from) and of text.js (cap, ll, tx, fact, say, art; links holds the card's LINKS sentences as 'source>key'). A Relic or a Deed has `as`, the card already in the game whose effect, cost and rules text it takes, and `fit`, one line on why the history suits that effect. src is the reference page for the card's dates, fact and links. Wikipedia could not be opened from the session that wrote the cards, so each card was checked through web search, which quotes Wikipedia and other pages; src2 is a second page the search quoted in support. sure is true when the search confirmed the card's dates, its fact and every link sentence, and false when it did not return one of them; check says what was not returned, or what the sources disagree about. Picture briefs (art) were written from memory and get the usual audit before any art is made. threads: named lines to collect, shaped like THREADS in cards.js. threadAdds: new cards that belong in a line cards.js already has. existing: links the new cards could give to cards already in the game (each needs a line in FROM or insp, and its sentence in LINKS). needsEngine: a few Relics and Deeds that are not among the 150, because each needs an effect the engine does not have. dropped: the cards that left the first draft, each with its reason. heldForGuides: five of those, kept whole, because a Guide's picture for each is on the working branch. merge: what the merge has to do that is not copying. Check with: node scripts/anoria/check-set-150.js

links.@library>euclid: Euclid taught and wrote in Alexandria in the years when its Library was being founded.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His Elements builds the whole of geometry, step by step, from a handful of plain starting points. It was copied, printed and taught from for more than two thousand years.
cards.art: Euclid about 300 BC in a shaded colonnade at Alexandria, teaching the first proof of his Elements: a spare Greek man of about fifty with a short grey beard, in a plain wool cloak, seated on a stone bench with a papyrus roll held open between his two hands, reading the next step aloud and glancing over the top of the roll. On the paving at his feet a young pupil kneels, swinging a cord pegged at one end to draw the second of two crossing circles in chalk, the triangle between them already ruled. Two more pupils lean in. The bright harbour shows between the columns. Seen from the pupil's side, low, so that Euclid's face and the roll are in the upper right. Nobody knows his face, so he is an ordinary Greek scholar of his day: no long white beard, no metal compasses with a hinge, no bound books. Keep the top left corner plain column and shadow.
cards.check: The search did not return that he worked in Alexandria under the first Ptolemy, or how long the Elements was taught from. Both are standard, written from memory.

links.archimedes>eratosthenes: Archimedes addressed his book The Method to his friend Eratosthenes.

cards.cap: Cyrene and Alexandria, c. 276 to c. 194 BC
cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: He worked out the distance around the Earth from the length of a shadow in Alexandria at noon on midsummer's day, when the Sun stood straight overhead in a town far to the south. His answer was close to the true one.
cards.art: Eratosthenes at noon on midsummer's day about 240 BC, measuring the Earth from a courtyard in Alexandria: a Greek scholar of about thirty-five, clean-shaven, in a light linen tunic with a cloak over one arm, down on one knee beside a bronze sundial bowl set on a low pillar, a hollow half-sphere with an upright pin at its centre. He is marking the tip of the pin's short shadow on the inside of the bowl with a reed pen, squinting against the glare, and his other hand shades his eyes. A boy holds an inkpot and a wax tablet. The sun is almost straight overhead, so every shadow in the white courtyard is small and sharp. Seen from the far side of the bowl, his face in the upper right. Ptolemaic Alexandria: no telescope, no globe, no glass lenses. Keep the top left corner bare sunlit wall.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: He and his school taught that illness has natural causes, and that a doctor should watch the patient closely and note what happens day by day. Many new doctors still take an oath that carries his name.
cards.art: Hippocrates on the island of Kos about 400 BC, examining a patient in the open air: an old man with a bald crown and a short white beard, as the ancient busts named for him show, in a plain cloak that leaves one shoulder bare, bending with his ear laid flat against the bare back of a fisherman who sits on a stool, listening to the man's breathing with his eyes shut and one hand raised for quiet. Two students stand by, one with a wax tablet and stylus ready, the other holding a bowl and a sponge. They are in the dappled shade of a huge plane tree in a small harbour town. Seen from the side, from the waist up, the old doctor's head in the upper right. Classical Greece: no serpent staff, no white coat, no surgery or blood. Keep the top left corner leaves and sky.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: In 132 he showed the Han court a bronze urn ringed with eight dragons, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad. When the ground shook far away one ball dropped, and it is said to have marked an earthquake days before riders brought the news.
cards.art: Zhang Heng, court astronomer of the Han dynasty, about AD 138, at the moment his earthquake urn proves itself: a slender scholar of sixty with a thin grey beard, in a long dark robe with wide sleeves, a sash and the tall lacquered cap of a Han official, standing with one hand raised and his head turned sharply toward a great bronze vessel shaped like a wine jar, as tall as a man. Eight bronze dragon heads point down around its shoulder, each with a ball in its jaws, and eight bronze toads squat below with their mouths open. One ball is in mid-air, falling from a dragon into a toad. Two junior officials have dropped their bamboo slips and stare. A timber hall with red pillars. Seen from across the vessel, Zhang Heng's face in the upper right. Eastern Han China: writing on bamboo slips and silk, no paper books, no chairs. Keep the top left corner dark roof beams.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: An official of the Han court, he reported to the emperor in 105 a way of making paper from tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn-out fishing nets. Paper of a rougher kind was older, but his was cheap and good enough to write on, and it spread across China.
cards.art: Cai Lun, an official of the imperial workshops of Han China, in AD 105: a beardless man of about fifty, as a palace eunuch was, in a plain belted robe with the sleeves tied back, standing at a wooden vat of grey pulp and lifting out with both hands a square bamboo frame stretched with cloth, water streaming from it and a thin even sheet of wet paper lying on the cloth. He tilts it to the light to judge it. Behind him workers pound bark and rags in a stone mortar, and a long row of the same frames leans against a sunlit wall to dry, each with its pale sheet. Seen from across the vat, from the waist up, his face in the upper right and the dripping frame at the centre. Eastern Han China: no printed pages, no bound books, no writing on the sheets. Keep the top left corner plain wall.
cards.check: His birth year is given as anything from 50 to 62, so the caption gives only his death.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His book of 628 is the first we know that treats zero as a number like any other, with rules for adding, taking away and multiplying with it. It speaks of numbers below zero as debts, and numbers above it as fortunes.
cards.art: Brahmagupta at thirty, in AD 628, an astronomer of western India, timing the rising of the Moon from a flat stone roof at dusk: a lean man with his hair tied in a knot on top of his head and a short beard, bare to the waist with a cotton shawl over one shoulder and a wrapped lower cloth. He sits cross-legged, sighting along a straight staff set upright on the parapet toward a huge moon just clearing the horizon, one hand lifted to give the signal. Beside him a pupil watches a water clock, a small copper bowl with a hole in its base slowly sinking in a larger basin, and keeps the count with pebbles. A bundle of palm-leaf pages tied between two boards lies by his knee. Seen from close by on the roof, his face in the upper right. India of the seventh century: palm-leaf pages, no paper books, no telescope, no turban of later centuries. Keep the top left corner darkening sky.
cards.check: The search confirmed the rules for zero and negative numbers; the words debts and fortunes were not returned.

links.brahmagupta>alkhwarizmi: Al-Khwarizmi's star tables follow the Sindhind, an Arabic version of Indian astronomy that is thought to come from Brahmagupta's book, and his own book on Indian numerals taught readers of Arabic to reckon with zero.

cards.tx: Legacy of Brahmagupta. Your Deeds cost 1 less.
cards.fact: His book on solving equations, written in Baghdad about 820, gave algebra its name, from the Arabic word al-jabr in its title. The word algorithm comes from his own name.
cards.art: Al-Khwarizmi about AD 820, on a canal bank outside the round city of Baghdad, putting his new method to work: a scholar of about forty with a full dark beard, in a long plain robe and a neatly wound turban, standing on the raised earth bank with a small wooden writing board held against his chest, a reed pen in his other hand, looking up from his reckoning to call a figure to two surveyors below who are stretching a knotted measuring rope across a field between stakes. A farmer and his brother wait at the field's edge for the answer that will divide their inheritance. Date palms, the canal, and far behind the wall of the city. Seen from the bank, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Abbasid Iraq: no chalkboard of modern symbols, no x and y, no Ottoman dress. Keep the top left corner pale sky.
cards.check: That the Sindhind comes from Brahmagupta's book is generally presumed, not proven; the link says so.

links.alkhwarizmi>fibonacci: Fibonacci learned the Indian numerals as a boy in North Africa, and his book draws on al-Khwarizmi and the Arab mathematicians who followed him.

cards.tx: Legacy of Al-Khwarizmi. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: His book of 1202 showed the merchants of Europe how to reckon with the nine Indian figures and zero in place of Roman numerals. One of its puzzles, about a pair of breeding rabbits, gives the string of numbers that now bears his name.
cards.art: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, about 1202, in a merchant's counting house in Pisa: a man of about thirty with dark hair cut straight across the brow and no beard, in a long belted tunic and a soft cap, standing at a sloping desk and writing a column of Indian numerals with a quill, quick and sure, while he holds up his left hand to stop an older merchant beside him who is still pushing counters about on a lined counting board. The older man stares at the finished sum. Sacks, a pair of scales and bolts of cloth fill the room, and through the open arch behind stands the cathedral's new bell tower, only three storeys built and already leaning. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, Fibonacci's face in the upper right. Pisa about 1200: no printed books, no eyeglasses, the tower unfinished. Keep the top left corner plain stone wall.

links.press>gutenberg: Gutenberg built his press in Mainz about 1450 and printed his great Bible on it.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: A goldsmith by training, he worked out how to cast metal letters by the thousand, all alike, in a small mould held in the hand. About 180 copies of his Bible were printed, and nearly fifty of them still exist.
cards.art: Johannes Gutenberg about 1450 in his workshop at Mainz, casting type: a man in his fifties in a plain dark gown with the sleeves rolled and a leather apron, a close cap on his head, standing by a small brick furnace. In his left hand he holds a little two-part mould of wood and iron that he has just snapped open, and a single bright new metal letter is dropping from it into his right palm; he peers at it closely. A ladle rests in the pot of molten metal, and on the bench are rows of finished letters, a file and a punch. Deep in the room behind, out of focus, stands the wooden press. Firelight on his face and hands. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No portrait of him from life exists, so the face is an ordinary craftsman's: no long forked beard, no fur hat. Keep the top left corner dark beams.

cards.tx: Voyager. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: He left Spain in 1519 with five ships and about 270 men to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. He was killed in the Philippines, and three years after setting out a single ship came home with eighteen of the crew, the first to sail around the world.
cards.art: Ferdinand Magellan in March 1518 at Valladolid, persuading the young king of Spain: a short, thickset Portuguese of about thirty-eight with a heavy dark beard and a lame left leg, in a plain black doublet and cap, standing with a painted globe held in the crook of one arm and the forefinger of his other hand laid on the blank place at the foot of South America where he believes a strait must be. He looks straight up at the king, who is only a slim shape on a dais at the upper left edge, with a bishop bending to whisper to him. Beside Magellan a cosmographer unrolls a sea chart. A bare Castilian hall with a coffered ceiling. Seen from beside the dais, so that Magellan faces us from the waist up, his face and the globe in the upper right. Spain in 1518: no ruffs, no armour, the globe showing no Pacific islands. Keep the top left corner dark ceiling.
cards.check: The globe shown to the king in 1518 and his lame leg are in the picture brief only and were not returned by the search.

links.copernicus>kepler: Kepler's first book, printed in 1596, was a defence of Copernicus's Sun-centred system.

cards.tx: Legacy of Copernicus. Scholar.
cards.fact: Working for years through another astronomer's sightings of Mars, he found that the planets move in ovals, not circles, and travel faster when they are nearer the Sun. He also defended his own mother in court when she was accused of witchcraft, and she went free.
cards.art: Johannes Kepler in Prague about 1605, at the end of his long war with the planet Mars: a thin, slight man of thirty-three with a pointed dark beard, in a black doublet with a small white collar, bent very close over a huge sheet of paper, for his eyes were weak, drawing with a pen the long oval path of a planet with the Sun set to one side of its centre. His free hand presses flat a stack of pages filled edge to edge with columns of figures, and more discarded pages cover the floor. The candles have burned down and grey dawn shows at a small leaded window; a brass quadrant hangs on the wall. Seen from across the table, low, his face in the upper right. Prague in 1605: he has no telescope yet, no globe of the planets, no wig. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.tx: Voyager: she can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Living in Constantinople as the British ambassador's wife, she saw old women guard children against smallpox by scratching a little matter from a mild case into the skin. She had her own son treated in 1718, and back in London she pressed doubting doctors to try it.
cards.art: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in Constantinople in March 1718, having her son protected against smallpox: an Englishwoman of twenty-eight with dark hair, her face lightly pitted by the smallpox she survived and her eyelashes gone, wearing the Turkish dress she adopted and was painted in, a long fitted coat of patterned silk over a fine shift and loose trousers, a small jewelled cap. She kneels on a carpet holding her five-year-old son firmly on her lap, his sleeve rolled to the shoulder, her eyes fixed on the work. An old Greek woman in a dark headscarf bends over the boy's arm with a needle in one hand and half a walnut shell in the other. A window shows domes and cypress trees. Seen from close, Lady Mary's face in the upper right. Ottoman Constantinople in 1718: no harem fantasy, no veils over faces, no doctor's instruments of a later age. Keep the top left corner plain wall.
cards.check: The year 1718 for her son's inoculation was not returned.

links.newton>duchatelet: Émilie du Châtelet put Newton's Principia into French, and hers is still the standard French translation.

cards.tx: Legacy of Isaac Newton. Scholar.
cards.fact: She translated Newton's great book from Latin into French and added pages of her own to explain its mathematics. She finished the work in 1749, only days before she died.
cards.art: Émilie du Châtelet in the summer of 1749, working through the night to finish her translation of Newton: a tall woman of forty-two with a long, lively face and dark hair loosely dressed and unpowdered, in a loose silk morning gown with the sleeves pushed back, seated at a table crowded with candles. A great Latin folio stands open on a reading stand before her; she writes fast on a sheet with her right hand while her left holds a pair of brass dividers stepped across a diagram of an orbit. Finished pages lie in a deep pile at her elbow, tied in bundles with ribbon, and a cold cup of coffee stands forgotten. A tall window is black with night. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. France in the 1740s: no towering wig, no court hoops, no chalkboard. Keep the top left corner dark panelled wall.

links.montagu>jenner: As a boy, Jenner was himself protected against smallpox by the method Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had brought to England.

cards.tx: Legacy of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: In 1796 he scratched matter from a milkmaid's cowpox sore into a boy's arm and showed that the boy could no longer catch smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin for cow, and in 1980 smallpox became the first human disease to be wiped out everywhere.
cards.art: Edward Jenner in May 1796 in a Gloucestershire dairy, studying the hand of the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes: a country doctor about to turn forty-seven with a round, kindly face and his own brown hair tied back, in a blue coat, yellow waistcoat and riding boots, holding the young woman's right hand in both of his and turning it to the light from the door to look at the blisters of cowpox on her fingers. She stands in a cap and apron, patient and a little amused. Behind them a brown and white cow turns her head in the stall, and a milking stool and wooden pail stand in the straw. A leather pocket case lies open on a barrel. Seen from inside the shed, from the waist up, Jenner's face in the upper right. England in the 1790s: no syringe, no white coat, no powdered court wig. Keep the top left corner dark timber.

cards.tx: Voyager. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: For five years he explored South and Central America, measuring everything from the heat of the sea to the blue of the sky. In 1802 he climbed higher on the volcano Chimborazo than anyone on record had ever climbed.
cards.art: Alexander von Humboldt on 23 June 1802, high on the volcano Chimborazo in the Andes, at the crack in the ridge that stopped him: a slim man of thirty-two with windblown light brown hair, in an ordinary town coat, waistcoat and thin boots cut to pieces by the rock, his lips and gums bleeding from the thin air. He kneels on a knife-edge of black rock and snow, holding a long glass barometer upright in its case and reading it with fierce attention, while a companion steadies the foot of the instrument and a third man writes the figure with numb fingers. Cloud boils below them on both sides and the white dome of the summit hangs close above. Seen from just along the ridge, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No ropes, ice axes or climbing clothes of later times, no fur. Keep the top left corner cloud.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: She was twelve when she and her brother dug an ichthyosaur out of the sea cliffs near their home, and she went on to find the first complete plesiosaur. She sold fossils for a living, and the learned men who bought them seldom gave her the credit.
cards.art: Mary Anning in December 1823 on the shore below the dark cliffs of Lyme Regis, uncovering the first complete plesiosaur: a sturdy young woman of twenty-four with a weathered face, in a heavy wool cloak, a long plain dress with mud to the knees and a bonnet tied down with a scarf, kneeling on a ledge of grey shale just washed bare by a winter storm. With a small hammer and chisel she is freeing the long line of neck bones that runs across the ledge to a tiny skull, and she has stopped, hammer lifted, to look at how long the neck is. A basket of tools stands beside her and her small black and white dog sits watching. Grey sea, wet rock, a landslip of clay behind. Seen from the seaward side, her face in the upper right, the fossil running down to the lower left. England in the 1820s: no dinosaur shown alive, no magnifying lens, no trousers. Keep the top left corner cliff and sky.

links.rosetta>champollion: The Rosetta Stone, with its Greek text beside the Egyptian, gave Champollion the way in to reading hieroglyphs.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: As a schoolboy he taught himself one ancient language after another, among them Coptic, the last form of ancient Egyptian. In 1822 he worked out how to read hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for some fourteen centuries.
cards.art: Jean-François Champollion at noon on 14 September 1822, in his attic study in Paris, at the instant he understands the hieroglyphs: a dark, curly-haired man of thirty-one with a full face, in shirtsleeves and an open waistcoat, half risen from his chair so suddenly that it is tipping over behind him. In one hand he grips a sheet of paper copied from a temple wall, on which a ring of picture signs is drawn in ink, a sun disc first among them; his other hand is flat on the table among dictionaries and sheets of the same signs set out in rows. His mouth is open in a shout. Sunlight from a small window falls across the papers. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Paris in 1822: no pith helmet, no pyramids through the window, no mummy. Keep the top left corner sloping attic ceiling.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: In a British army hospital in the Crimean War she fought for clean wards, fresh air and decent food, and far fewer soldiers died. She was also a gifted statistician, and drew a new kind of chart to show that dirt and disease were killing more men than battle.
cards.art: Florence Nightingale in the winter of 1854 on her night round of the army hospital at Scutari: a slender woman of thirty-four with a calm, firm face and brown hair parted in the middle under a small white cap, in a plain black wool dress with a white collar and a short dark cape. She carries the lamp she really used, a Turkish lantern of folded waxed cloth like a small concertina with a metal top and base and a candle inside, held low at her side so that its glow lights her face from below. She has stopped at one of the low beds that line an endless corridor and bends to lay two fingers on the wrist of a sleeping soldier. The rows of beds vanish into the dark behind her. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. No brass oil lamp with a spout, no nurse's apron with a red cross, no starched veil. Keep the top left corner darkness.

links.jenner>pasteur: Pasteur gave his own method the name vaccination, in honour of Jenner's work with cowpox.

cards.tx: Legacy of Edward Jenner. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He showed that germs spoil food and cause disease, and that gentle heat kills them, which is why milk is pasteurised. In 1885 his new vaccine saved a nine-year-old boy who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog.
cards.art: Louis Pasteur in July 1885 in his laboratory in Paris, on the day the boy Joseph Meister is first treated: a grey-bearded man of sixty-two with a grave, anxious face, in a dark coat and a small black skullcap, his left arm held a little stiffly at his side. He stands with his right hand resting on the shoulder of a nine-year-old boy in a short jacket, whose bandaged hands and leg show the dog bites, and he watches without blinking as a doctor in the background draws liquid into a small glass syringe. On the bench beside them stand glass flasks with long bent necks and a tall jar in which a strip of dried tissue hangs from a thread. Daylight from a high window. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, Pasteur's face in the upper right, the boy lower and to the left. France in the 1880s: no white coats, no microscope held to the eye, no electric light. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

links.verne>bly: Nellie Bly set out in 1889 to beat the eighty days of Jules Verne's novel, and stopped in France on the way to meet him.

cards.tx: Voyager. Swift: she can walk on the turn she arrives.
cards.fact: A newspaper reporter, she went around the world alone in 1889 and 1890 with one small bag, by steamer, train, rickshaw and donkey, in seventy-two days. Two years earlier she had pretended to be mad to get herself locked in an asylum for ten days, and wrote about the cruelty she found there.
cards.art: Nellie Bly in January 1890 on the last leg of her race around the world, crossing America by special train: a small, quick young woman of twenty-five with a fringe of dark hair, in the one dress she took, plain dark blue wool, under a long checked travelling coat, a peaked cloth cap on her head. She stands on the open rear platform of a railway carriage with one hand gripping the iron rail and the other holding up a small leather handbag, the only luggage she carried, laughing into the wind as the track streams away behind. On a prairie station platform slipping past, a crowd waves hats and handkerchiefs. Steam and snow. Seen from the trackside, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. America in 1890: no trunk, no parasol, no bustle, no hot-air balloon (there is none in the book or in her journey). Keep the top left corner steam and sky.

links.faraday>tesla: Tesla's motors run on electromagnetic induction, the effect that Faraday discovered.

cards.tx: On arrival, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He designed the alternating-current motors and power system that still carry electricity to homes around the world. On the lecture stage he made glass lamps glow with no wire leading to them.
cards.art: Nikola Tesla about 1892, lecturing in a darkened hall: a very tall, very thin man of thirty-six with black hair parted in the middle and a neat moustache, in a black tailcoat and white tie, standing alone on the stage with his arms lifted and spread. In each bare hand he holds a long glass tube with no wire leading to it, and both tubes are glowing with a cold white light that is the only light in the picture, throwing his face and shirt front into sharp relief. Behind him, half seen, stand two tall metal sheets on insulated posts and a table of coils. The front rows of the audience are dark shapes of heads at the bottom edge. Seen from the stalls, from the knees up, his face in the upper half, right of centre. Accounts of these lectures differ on whether he held the glowing tubes or they hung in the air between the sheets, so check before the picture is made. No lightning bolts leaping about the room, no tower, no goggles. Correct anatomy, two hands, each holding one tube. Keep the top left corner darkness.

One search summary said his lamps glowed in the field between two plates and were not held in his hands, so the fact now says only that they glowed with no wire, and the picture brief asks for a check. The link to Faraday is physics, not checked.

cards.tx: Legacy of Isaac Newton or Michael Faraday. He has +1 Might for each Legacy line on your side, up to +2.
cards.fact: In 1905, while he worked as a clerk in the Swiss patent office, he published four papers that changed physics, one of them on relativity. He was twenty-six.
cards.art: Albert Einstein in 1905, aged twenty-six, at his desk in the patent office in Bern: a sturdy young man with thick dark curly hair, a dark moustache and large brown eyes, in a checked wool suit with a stiff collar and tie, standing at a high sloping clerk's desk on which a patent drawing of some electrical machine is pinned. He has stopped work; his pen hangs loose in his fingers and his head is turned to the tall window, where over the roofs of the old town a tram is drawing away down the street from a medieval clock tower with a great painted dial. He is looking at the clock and the tram, lost in a thought. Under the drawing lies a hidden sheet of his own notes. Seen from inside the office, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. He is a young man: no white hair, no rumpled sweater, no blackboard, no formula written anywhere. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

links.ada>turing: In 1950 Turing answered what he called Lady Lovelace's Objection, her remark that a machine can do only what we know how to order it to do.

cards.tx: Legacy of Ada Lovelace. On arrival, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: At twenty-four he described, on paper, a single machine that could carry out any calculation, the idea behind every computer since. In the Second World War he designed machines that broke Germany's Enigma code day after day.
cards.art: Alan Turing in 1940, on a night shift in a wooden hut at Bletchley Park: a young man of twenty-eight with dark hair falling over his forehead and deep-set blue eyes, in a tweed jacket with a pullover and a carelessly knotted tie, sitting sideways on a hard chair at a trestle table. He holds a long sheet of paper punched with rows of holes up against a desk lamp and looks through it, lining it against a second sheet. On the table are stacks of messages in five-letter groups, pencils, and a cipher machine like a typewriter in an open wooden box, with three small wheels at the top. Behind him his tea mug is fastened to the radiator pipe by a small chain and padlock. Blackout curtains at the window. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Britain in 1940: no computer screens, no modern keyboards, no uniform. Keep the top left corner plain board wall.

cards.fact: He built the largest empire the world had yet seen, and let the peoples he conquered keep their own gods and customs. A clay cylinder found at Babylon records, in his name, that he sent exiled peoples home.
cards.art: Cyrus, king of Persia, entering Babylon in October of 539 BC without a battle: a man of about sixty with a full, squared grey beard and long hair, in a long pleated Persian robe with wide sleeves, a simple band of gold around his brow, walking on foot and bare-headed under the towering blue-glazed Ishtar Gate with its rows of golden bulls and dragons. He holds his right hand open at shoulder height in greeting, and his sheathed short sword hangs untouched at his belt. cards.fact: A chief's son of the Cherusci, he had served as an officer with the Roman army and knew how it fought. In AD 9 he drew three legions into forest and bog in the rain and destroyed them, and Rome gave up its plan to rule the lands beyond the Rhine.
cards.art: Arminius in September of AD 9, aged about twenty-six, at the edge of the forest on the morning he turns on Rome: a tall young German noble with reddish-fair hair combed to one side and tied in a knot above his temple, a short beard, and the mail shirt and long cavalry sword of a Roman officer of the allied horse, which he has been. He has reined in out of sight of the marching column, dismounted, and is pulling the red Roman officer's cloak from his shoulders with one hand to let it fall in the mud, while with the other he grips the forearm of an older chief in a wool cloak and trousers who has stepped from the trees. Behind the chief the wood is full of half-seen warriors with spears and long narrow shields. Rain, dripping oaks, wet ferns. Seen from between the trees, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No winged or horned helmets, no fur loincloths, no battle yet. Keep the top left corner dark leaves.
cards.check: His Roman service, the three legions and AD 9 were confirmed. The search did not return the words Suetonius gives Augustus (Suetonius, Augustus 23).

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: Trưng Trắc and her sister Trưng Nhị raised northern Vietnam against its Chinese rulers in AD 40 and took sixty-five towns. They ruled as queens for about three years, and Vietnam still honours them every year.
cards.art: The two Trưng sisters, Trắc and Nhị, in the spring of AD 40 at the mouth of the Hát River in northern Vietnam, calling their people to rise: two young noblewomen of the Lạc people, the elder a little taller, with their hair wound up in cloth, in wrapped skirts and short jackets with broad woven belts, each with a short bronze sword at her side. They stand on a river bluff on either side of a great bronze drum that reaches to their waists, its flat top cast with a many-pointed star and rings of flying birds; the elder sister is bringing a wooden mallet down on the star with both hands, and the younger holds a spear upright and looks out over the water. Below them long war canoes crowded with men and women are pulling in to the bank from every side. Seen from just below the bluff, both sisters from the knees up, their faces in the upper half, right of centre. Vietnam two thousand years ago: no elephants in this picture, no silk court robes of later dynasties, no conical hats. Keep the top left corner river mist.

cards.tx: Raider: she has +2 Might when she attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: Queen of the desert trading city of Palmyra, she took Egypt and much of the Roman East in two years and ruled it in her young son's name. Scholars were welcome at her court, and she was said to speak several languages.
cards.art: Zenobia, queen of Palmyra, about AD 270, sending her army out to Egypt along the city's great colonnaded street: a dark-eyed woman of about thirty with a strong, intent face, dressed as the carved portraits of Palmyra's noblewomen show them, in a long embroidered tunic with a cloak pinned at the left shoulder by a large brooch, a jewelled band across her forehead under a wound headcloth, heavy earrings and many bracelets. She stands on the steps at the foot of a four-pillared monument with a soldier's helmet held in the crook of her arm and her other hand lifted in salute. Past her down the street, between two endless rows of tall honey-coloured columns, rides her heavy cavalry, men and horses alike covered in scale armour, with long lances. Seen from the roadway, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Roman Syria: no chains, no Roman triumph, no belly-dancer costume, no veil across the face. Keep the top left corner column tops and sky.

links.eleanor>richard: Richard was Eleanor's son. While he was held prisoner in 1193 she gathered the ransom that freed him.
links.saladin>richard: Richard and Saladin fought over the Holy Land for more than a year and made peace in 1192 without ever meeting face to face.

cards.tx: Legacy of Eleanor of Aquitaine. Raider: he has +2 Might when he attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: King of England for ten years, he spent barely six months of them there. He led the Third Crusade to within a day's march of Jerusalem and then turned back, judging that he could take the city but never hold it.
cards.art: Richard, king of England, in June 1192 on a hilltop in Judea, within sight of Jerusalem and deciding to turn back: a very tall man of thirty-four with red-gold hair and a short beard, in a long shirt of mail with the mail hood pushed back on his shoulders, a plain linen surcoat over it and a sword belt, dusty and sunburned. He stands with his long kite-shaped shield lifted in his left hand so that its rim hides the far skyline from his own eyes, his head turned aside behind it, as an old story says he did, refusing to look at the city he could not take. Beyond the edge of the shield we can see what he will not: small pale walls and a dome on a distant ridge. A few of his knights wait behind with their horses, silent. Seen from in front and a little below, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. The twelfth century: no plate armour, no closed great helm, no three lions on the shield, no crown. Keep the top left corner hard blue sky.
cards.check: That he spent about six months of his reign in England was not returned.

links.magellan>lapulapu: Magellan was killed in 1521 on the island of Mactan, fighting the warriors of its chief Lapulapu.

cards.tx: At home he has +3 Might instead of +1.
cards.fact: Chief of the small island of Mactan in the Philippines, he would not bow to the king of Spain. When Magellan waded ashore in 1521 to force him, Lapulapu's warriors met the armoured Spaniards in the shallows and Magellan was killed.
cards.art: Lapulapu, chief of Mactan, at dawn on 27 April 1521, waiting on his own beach for the strangers to come ashore: a lean, hard man in the prime of life (his age is not recorded), his long hair tied back under a red cloth wound around his head, his chest, arms and legs covered in fine dark tattooed patterns, as the Spanish wrote of the islanders, with gold ornaments in his ears, a loincloth with a long embroidered end and a sash. He stands at the water's edge with a long narrow wooden shield on his left arm and a heavy single-edged sword that widens toward its tip held low in his right hand, perfectly still. Behind him his warriors are drawn up in three bodies with bamboo spears whose points are hardened in fire. Far out, beyond a reef that their boats cannot cross, men in steel helmets are climbing down into waist-deep water. Seen from the shallows, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. The Visayas in 1521: no feather headdress, no carved masks, no grass skirt. Keep the top left corner dawn sky and palm fronds.
cards.check: Nothing shows that Lapulapu himself struck Magellan; the card does not say so. His age is not recorded.

cards.tx: He has +2 Might when he attacks a stronger Figure.
cards.fact: He fought his first duel at thirteen and, by his own count, won more than sixty without a defeat. Late in life he was also a painter, and in a cave he wrote down his way of the sword as The Book of Five Rings.
cards.art: Miyamoto Musashi in April 1612, aged about twenty-eight, on his way to the most famous duel of his life, as the old accounts tell it: a big, rough-looking swordsman with unshaven cheeks and long uncombed hair tied back with a strip of cloth, in a plain dark kimono with the sleeves tied up by a cord across his back. He sits in the bow of a small fishing boat rowed by one old boatman, shaving the blade of a spare oar into a long wooden sword with his short sword, curls of wood falling into the water, his eyes not on his hands but on the shore ahead. On a small flat island across the strait a tiny figure waits on the beach with a very long sword, and banners flutter behind him. Low morning sun in the rower's eyes. Seen from the water in front of the boat, Musashi from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Early Edo Japan: no armour, no ninja, no two swords drawn. Keep the top left corner glare and sky.
cards.check: The sword carved from an oar is from the old accounts and was not returned.

cards.tx: Guard: enemies here must clash with him first.
cards.fact: He was the last leader of Palmares, a country of villages in the hills of Brazil built by people who had escaped slavery, which held out against Portuguese armies for most of a century. Brazil keeps the day of his death, 20 November, as Black Awareness Day.
cards.art: Zumbi, leader of Palmares, about 1690, on the wooden wall of its hilltop capital in the forest of north-east Brazil: a strong Black man in his mid thirties with a short beard and a grave, alert face, in a loose cotton shirt, knee breeches and a cloth sash, a long iron-headed lance in his hand and a knife in his belt. He is on the fighting step behind a palisade of sharpened tree trunks, one hand shading his eyes, looking down the steep slope over the tops of palms to where a thread of smoke shows an army on the march. Along the wall men and women are passing up bows, baskets of stones and a few muskets, and behind them lie thatched houses, a forge and fields of maize. Seen from on the wall, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No portrait of him exists: no chains, no loincloth costume, no crown. Keep the top left corner palm crowns and sky.
cards.check: Sources count Palmares from about 1605 to 1694.

cards.cap: Blue Mountains, Jamaica, c. 1686 to c. 1760
cards.tx: Raider: she has +2 Might when she attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: She led the Windward Maroons, people who had freed themselves from slavery and lived in Jamaica's Blue Mountains, where British soldiers hunted them for years and could not beat them. A grant of 1740 gave her and her people their own land, and her face is on Jamaica's five-hundred-dollar note.
cards.art: Nanny, leader of the Windward Maroons, about 1733, on a ridge of the Blue Mountains of Jamaica above a column of British soldiers: a small, wiry Black woman of middle age with a fierce, still face, her head tied in a cloth, in a plain wrapped dress of coarse blue cotton with a knife at her belt and strings of beads at her neck. She crouches behind a rock at the lip of a gorge with a cow's horn raised to her lips, sounding the signal, her other hand held out flat behind her to hold back the fighters who lie hidden along the ridge, men and women so covered in tied-on leaves and branches that they look like bushes. Far below on a narrow path beside a river, a file of redcoats toils upward, tiny, looking the wrong way. Mist, tree ferns, wet green light. Seen from along the ridge, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. Jamaica in the 1730s: no chains, no witch's props, no torches. Keep the top left corner mist and leaves.
cards.check: The banknote was not returned. Her dates are estimates.

cards.tx: Inspiring. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He kept a ragged army together through eight years of war against Britain, then gave up his command and went home to his farm. After two terms as the first president he stepped down again, and set the custom that no president rules for life.
cards.art: George Washington on 23 December 1783 at Annapolis, giving up command of the army now that the war is won: a very tall, big-boned man of fifty-one with a long, strong face and his own reddish-brown hair powdered and tied back, in the dark blue coat with buff facings and gold epaulettes of the Continental Army, buff breeches and black boots. He stands in the middle of a plain assembly room and holds out a folded paper, his commission, toward a seated row of congressmen who have kept their hats on; the paper trembles a little in his hand and his face is tight with feeling. Men and women crowd the gallery above, several of them in tears. Winter light from tall windows. Seen from beside the congressmen, so that he faces us from the knees up, his face in the upper right. America in 1783: no white horse, no crossing of a river, no sword drawn, no white curled wig. Keep the top left corner gallery rail and wall.
cards.check: The two terms were not returned.

links.hannibal>napoleon: When Napoleon took his army over the Alps in 1800, his painter set Hannibal's name on the rocks beside his own.
links.caesar>napoleon: In his last years on Saint Helena, Napoleon dictated a book on the wars of Julius Caesar.

cards.tx: Legacy of Hannibal or Julius Caesar. He has +2 Might while you have more Figures here than the other player.
cards.fact: An artillery officer from the island of Corsica, he made himself emperor of the French at thirty-five and for ten years beat almost every army sent against him. The code of laws drawn up under him is still the base of the law in France and in many other countries.
cards.art: Napoleon on the night of 1 December 1805, the eve of the battle of Austerlitz, walking through his army's camp: a man of thirty-six of ordinary height with a pale, full face and short dark hair, in a plain grey overcoat buttoned over a green uniform, a black two-cornered hat worn sideways across his head, his hands clasped behind his back. He walks along a frozen track between the bivouac fires, and as the soldiers know him they are leaping up, twisting the straw of their bedding into torches, lighting them at the fires and holding them high, so that a river of flame runs away into the dark on both sides of him. He looks at the men, half smiling. Tall fur caps, long muskets, breath steaming. Seen from in front on the track, from the knees up, his face lit gold in the upper right. France in 1805: no white horse, no hand tucked in his coat, no crown or robes. Keep the top left corner night sky.
cards.check: Emperor at 35, the Code and the names on the rocks of David's painting were confirmed. The search did not return the book on Caesar's wars that he dictated on Saint Helena (Précis des guerres de César, printed 1836).

cards.tx: Voyager. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: Ordered off their homeland in 1877, he and the Nez Perce travelled about 1,170 miles toward Canada with their families and herds, fighting off the United States Army again and again. They were stopped forty miles short of the border.
cards.art: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce in the late summer of 1877, leading the families of his people over a mountain pass on their long retreat: a tall, heavy-shouldered man of thirty-seven with a broad, grave face, his hair swept up in a high roll above the forehead with a long braid hanging in front of each shoulder, shell earrings, a striped trade blanket wrapped around him over a cloth shirt, leggings and beaded moccasins. He walks on foot at the head of a file, leading a spotted horse on which a small girl sits in front of an old woman, and he is looking back over his shoulder down the line of people, pack horses and dragging lodge poles that winds away through fallen timber. Sleet is beginning; the peaks are white. Seen from the trail ahead, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. The Plateau peoples in 1877: no feathered war bonnet, no war paint, no rifle raised. Keep the top left corner grey sky and pines.

cards.tx: At home he has +3 Might instead of +1.
cards.fact: Emperor of Ethiopia, he armed and united his country while European powers were dividing up the rest of Africa. At Adwa in 1896 his army of up to a hundred thousand beat an invading Italian one, and Ethiopia stayed free.
cards.art: Menelik II, emperor of Ethiopia, at first light on 1 March 1896 above the valley of Adwa: a big, dark, bearded man of fifty-one with a broad pockmarked face, in the dress he wore on campaign, a black silk cape over white cotton robes and a wide-brimmed dark felt hat, standing on a rocky spur under a great red umbrella held by an attendant. He has a field glass lowered in one hand and with the other signals forward a battery of small mountain guns whose crews are dragging them into line. Around him stand his generals in lion's-mane collars and embroidered capes with round hide shields, and priests in white with tall processional crosses. Below, masses of white-robed riflemen pour down between strange steep towers of rock toward the gun flashes in the valley. Seen from on the spur, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Ethiopia in 1896: no spears only, no bare feet and loincloths, no European crown. Keep the top left corner rock peak and sky.
cards.check: Estimates of his army run from 73,000 to over 100,000.

cards.tx: She has +2 Might while she is outnumbered here.
cards.fact: When a British governor demanded the Golden Stool, the sacred seat that holds the soul of the Asante nation, the chiefs hesitated. Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu and about sixty years old, shamed them into fighting and led the war herself.
cards.art: Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, on the night of 28 March 1900 in Kumasi, at the secret council of the Asante chiefs: a small, upright woman of about sixty with a lined, fearless face and her hair cropped close in the round, high-shaved style of an Asante queen mother, wearing a rich patterned cloth wrapped under her arms with a second cloth over one shoulder, and sandals. She has risen from her stool and stands in the middle of the circle with her arm stretched out, pointing at the seated chiefs, who sit under their great fringed umbrellas with their eyes on the ground, gold rings on their fingers and their sword bearers behind them. A single lamp lights her from below. One young chief has begun to stand. Seen from within the circle, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. The Golden Stool itself is not in the picture and must not be shown: it is sacred and was hidden. No guns fired, no face paint. Keep the top left corner dark umbrella and night.
cards.check: Her age in 1900 is an estimate from a birth about 1840.

cards.tx: Swift: he can walk on the turn he arrives.
cards.fact: A member of the Sac and Fox Nation, he won both the pentathlon and the decathlon at the 1912 Olympics. Before one event his shoes went missing, and he competed in two odd ones, one of them picked out of a rubbish bin.
cards.art: Jim Thorpe in July 1912 at the Olympic Games in Stockholm, winning the last race of the decathlon: a powerfully built young man of twenty-five with thick black hair and a broad, determined face, in the white vest of the American team with a shield on the chest and white shorts, driving for the finish tape on a cinder track with his chest thrown forward. On his feet are two shoes that do not match, one larger than the other and worn over extra socks. The other runners are well behind him. A brick stadium with a clock tower and wooden stands hung with flags, and officials in straw hats along the track. Seen from just past the finish line, low, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. 1912: no starting blocks, no modern running shoes, no feathers or costume of any kind. Keep the top left corner stadium tower and sky.

cards.tx: Swift: he can walk on the turn he arrives.
cards.fact: At the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, where Germany's rulers meant to show that their own race was the best, he won four gold medals. A German long jumper, Luz Long, made friends with him in front of the whole crowd.
cards.art: Jesse Owens in August 1936 at the Olympic Games in Berlin, in the air above the long-jump pit: a slim, long-legged young Black man of twenty-two with a calm, open face, in the white vest of the American team with a red and blue stripe slanting across the chest and white shorts, caught at the top of his leap with both legs flung forward, his arms reaching past his knees and his eyes fixed on the sand far ahead. A measuring board runs along the pit, and an official in a white jacket crouches with a marker. On the grass beside the runway a tall fair-haired German jumper in a tracksuit is watching him and clapping. The huge stone stadium is packed to the sky behind. Seen from beside the pit, low, his whole figure in the upper half of the picture, his face right of centre. No flags or party emblems of any kind are shown. Correct anatomy, two arms, two legs. Keep the top left corner stadium rim and sky.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: Daughter of King Sargon and high priestess of the moon god at Ur, she wrote hymns in her own voice and put her name to them. She is the first author in history whose name we know.
cards.art: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god at Ur, about 2270 BC, composing a hymn at night, dressed as the carved stone disc that bears her own name shows her: a woman of about thirty-five with a strong profile and long hair falling down her back from under a round cap with a rolled brim, in a long robe of tiered woollen flounces that leaves one shoulder bare. She sits on a low stool on the flat roof of the temple house under a thin crescent moon, a small cushion-shaped tablet of damp clay in her left palm and a cut reed in her right hand, pressed to the clay; her lips are parted as she tries the line aloud. A lamp of oil burns in a shell beside her, and a servant waits with a basket of fresh clay. Below lie the mud-brick city and the palm groves along the river. Seen from the roof beside her, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. Early Mesopotamia: no great stepped tower yet (that was built two centuries later), no winged bulls, no Egyptian dress. Keep the top left corner night sky.

links.homer>aeschylus: An ancient writer reports that Aeschylus called his own plays slices from the great banquet of Homer.

cards.tx: Legacy of Homer. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He gave Greek plays a second actor, so that for the first time two people could argue face to face on the stage. He had fought the Persians at Marathon, and the words on his grave spoke of that and never mentioned his plays.
cards.art: Aeschylus in the spring of 472 BC, in the theatre under the Acropolis of Athens, rehearsing his play The Persians: a broad, weathered man of fifty-three with a bald crown, a full grey beard and the scarred forearms of an old soldier, in a plain cloak. He stands on the beaten earth of the dancing floor, lifting a painted linen mask with a tall crown, wide eyes and an open mouth, and settling it over the head of an actor who wears a long robe with sleeves in the Persian fashion; a second actor waits with his own mask in his hand. Behind them the chorus, twelve men in eastern dress, practise a slow step in rows, and a piper tunes a double pipe. The audience seats are plain wooden benches on the hillside. Seen from the dancing floor, from the waist up, the playwright's face in the upper right. Athens in 472 BC: no stone theatre, no raised stage, no comedy masks. Keep the top left corner hillside and sky.

cards.tx: Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: The best-loved poet of China's Tang dynasty, he wandered the country for most of his life, and about a thousand of his poems survive, many of them about friends, mountains, the Moon and wine. Legend says he drowned reaching from a boat to embrace the Moon's reflection.
cards.art: Li Bai about 744, drinking alone under the Moon, as in the best known of his poems: a man of forty-three with a free, handsome face, a thin beard and bright eyes, in the loose robe of a Tang gentleman with wide sleeves, a black gauze cap pushed back on his head and a straight sword at his belt. He stands among blossoming trees on a terrace on a mountainside, his head tilted back, raising a small wine cup high in his right hand toward the full moon as if inviting it to drink, and his left arm is flung out. The moonlight throws his long shadow across the white stones behind him, so that he, the Moon and the shadow make a party of three. A wine jar stands on a rock. Seen from below the terrace, from the knees up, his face in the upper right and the Moon high at the centre. Tang China: no boat, no drowning, no Japanese dress. Keep the top left corner blossom branches.
cards.check: The figure of about a thousand poems was not returned.

links.murasaki>seishonagon: Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shōnagon served rival empresses, and Murasaki wrote in her diary that Sei was dreadfully conceited.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when she arrives.
cards.fact: A lady at the Japanese court, she filled a notebook with lists of things that delighted or annoyed her, sharp stories about the people around her and what she saw from day to day. It is called The Pillow Book, and people have been reading it for a thousand years.
cards.art: Sei Shōnagon about the year 995, on a snowy morning in the empress's rooms in Kyoto, in the best-known scene of her Pillow Book: a quick-witted court lady of about thirty with a pale oval face and hair that falls to the floor, in many layers of silk robes whose coloured edges show at the neck and sleeves. The empress has asked what the snow looks like on a mountain in an old Chinese poem, and Sei, instead of answering, has gone to the outer wall and is rolling up a hanging blind of fine bamboo with both hands, so that the white garden outside suddenly floods the dim room with light. Behind her the young empress, half hidden by a curtain stand, laughs, and other ladies look up from a charcoal brazier. Seen from inside the room, Sei from the knees up, her face turned back toward us in the upper right. Heian Japan: no writing desk in this picture, no later kimono with a wide sash, no fan held open. Keep the top left corner dark ceiling.
cards.check: Some scholars think Sei had left court before Murasaki arrived; the link says only that they served rival empresses.

cards.tx: At the end of a round, if you hold his Place, draw a card.
cards.fact: He spent some thirty years writing the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, which tells the story of Persia from the creation of the world in about fifty thousand rhyming couplets. It is one of the longest poems ever written by one person, and it helped to keep the Persian language alive.
cards.art: Ferdowsi about the year 1010, aged seventy, in the orchard of his house at Tus in eastern Persia, setting down the last lines of the Book of Kings: an old country gentleman with a long white beard and a tired, satisfied face, in a long quilted robe with a sash and a white turban, sitting on a carpet under a mulberry tree with a board across his knees. He has just lifted his reed pen from the page and holds it in the air. All around him on the carpet, in an open chest and stacked in a niche of the garden wall, are tied bundles of written pages, the work of thirty years, hundreds of them. A boy pours water from a ewer; a single saddled horse waits at the gate. Composed like a Persian manuscript painting, with flat bright colour and a high horizon. Seen from the carpet, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Persia about the year 1000: no printed books, no heroes or monsters in the sky. Keep the top left corner leaves.
cards.check: Sources give 30 to 33 years and 50,000 to 60,000 couplets.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: A teacher of Islamic law in what is now Turkey, he began pouring out poems of love and longing for God after he met a wandering holy man named Shams. His followers became the Mevlevi order, known for a whirling dance that is a form of prayer.
cards.art: Rumi about 1250 in the goldsmiths' street of the market at Konya, in the story his followers told of how the turning dance began: a scholar of about forty-three with a brown beard and a rapt, lifted face, in a wide-sleeved robe and a large wound turban, who has stopped in the middle of the lane with his eyes closed, his right arm rising and his left arm falling, the skirts of his robe just beginning to swing out as he turns in time to the ringing of hammers. In the open-fronted shop beside him a goldbeater and his apprentices, seated at their anvils, have looked up but keep hammering, sheets of gold leaf shining on the bench. Passers-by stop with baskets on their heads. Seen from down the lane, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Seljuk Anatolia in the thirteenth century: no tall felt cap and white skirt of the later dervishes, no Ottoman dress. Keep the top left corner shop awning and shadow.
cards.check: The goldsmiths' hammers are tied to his ecstasy and to Salah al-Din Zarkub in the sources; that the turning began there is the order's own story (picture brief only).

cards.tx: At the end of a round, if you hold his Place, draw a card.
cards.fact: A soldier who lost the use of his left hand in a sea battle, he was later seized by pirates and held for five years in Algiers. He was in his late fifties when he published Don Quixote, the story of an old gentleman who reads too many tales of knights and sets out to be one.
cards.art: Miguel de Cervantes about 1600, a travelling tax collector in his early fifties, writing at an inn on the plain of La Mancha, with the face he described himself: an eagle's nose, chestnut hair, a smooth high forehead, a beard gone silver and large moustaches. He wears a worn black doublet with a small plain collar. He sits at a rough table by the inn's open door, writing with his right hand and holding the paper still with his left, which lies stiff and half closed, crippled by an old wound. He has looked up from the page and out of the door, amused, to where a thin old farmer on a bony horse and a stout man on a donkey are passing along the road in the heat, with a row of white windmills turning on the ridge behind them. A jug, bread, his saddlebags. Seen from inside the dark room, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Spain about 1600: no wide cartwheel ruff, no knight in full armour. Keep the top left corner dark rafters.

links.galileo>artemisia: Artemisia Gentileschi came to know Galileo in Florence, and the two wrote to each other for years afterwards.

cards.tx: She has +2 Might when she attacks a stronger Figure.
cards.fact: She was painting like a master at seventeen, and became the first woman admitted to the academy of art in Florence. Her pictures are known for strong women from old stories, caught in the middle of the action.
cards.art: Artemisia Gentileschi about 1638, at work, in the pose of her own self-portrait as the art of painting: a strong-armed woman of forty-five with a round face flushed with effort and dark hair coming loose from its knot, in a green silk dress with the sleeves pushed up above the elbow and a brown apron, a thin gold chain around her neck from which a tiny mask hangs. She leans steeply in from the right toward a tall canvas whose back is to us, her right arm stretched up and across with a long brush at its tip, her left hand low and holding a palette and more brushes, her eyes on a point of the canvas we cannot see. Hard light from a high window falls on her forehead, forearm and bare neck against a plain brown wall. Seen from close beside the easel, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. Nothing of the painted picture is shown. Italy in the 1630s: no beret, no smock of a later age. Keep the top left corner plain shadowed wall.
cards.check: Her death is given as 1653 or about 1656.

links.libai>basho: Bashō opens his travel diary by echoing Li Bai's line that the passing days and months are travellers too.

cards.tx: Legacy of Li Bai. Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: In 1689 he sold his house and set off on foot through the wild north of Japan, a journey of some 2,400 kilometres, writing as he went. His travel diary, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, is full of the three-line poems we call haiku.
cards.art: Matsuo Bashō in the summer of 1689, aged forty-five, shooting the rapids of the Mogami River in the far north of Japan, swollen with the early summer rains, as his travel diary tells: a slight, weathered man with a shaved head, in the black robe of a lay monk hitched up at the knees, straw sandals and a wide round hat of woven sedge tied under his chin. He kneels in the middle of a long, narrow flat-bottomed rice boat that is racing bow-down between green cliffs, one hand gripping the side and the other clamping his hat to his head, his mouth open in something between terror and delight. Behind him his companion clings to their bundles, and a boatman stands in the stern leaning his whole weight on a long pole. White water, a thread of waterfall down the cliff, rain. Seen from the bank just ahead of the boat, Bashō from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Edo Japan: no sword, no samurai topknot. Keep the top left corner wet cliff and leaves.
cards.check: The journey of 1689, its length and the echo of Li Bai in the opening were confirmed.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: At twenty he walked some 400 kilometres to hear a famous organist play, and stayed away about three months longer than his employers had allowed. He wrote more than a thousand pieces of music, and four of his sons became composers too.
cards.art: Johann Sebastian Bach in the late autumn of 1705, aged twenty, on his long walk across Germany to hear the old organist of Lübeck: a sturdy, square-faced young man with strong dark brows and his own brown hair tied back, in a long travelling coat, muddy boots and a broad hat, a leather satchel of music across his back and a stout stick in his hand. He has come over the last rise of a flat, wet road at sunset and stopped dead: ahead, across the marshes, stand the brick walls of the city and, above them, the two tall green spires of the great church he has walked three weeks to reach. He stares at them, breathing hard, with the beginning of a grin. A carter going the other way looks back at him. Seen from the road in front of him, from the knees up, his face in the upper right, the city small in the lower left. Germany in 1705: no white wig, no organ, no sheet music in his hand. Keep the top left corner evening sky.
cards.check: The count of his works and his sons were not returned.

links.homer>wheatley: The first poem in Phillis Wheatley's book opens by praising Homer.
links.virgil>wheatley: Phillis Wheatley learned Latin in her teens, and in the first poem of her book she wishes she could sing as Virgil did.

cards.tx: Legacy of Homer or Virgil. Scholar.
cards.fact: Seized in West Africa at about seven and sold in Boston, she was reading Latin poets within a few years. In 1773 she became the first African American to publish a book of poems, after eighteen leading men of Boston signed a paper saying that she had truly written them.
cards.art: Phillis Wheatley about 1772, aged about nineteen, writing late at night in the house in Boston where she was held as a slave, in the pose of the portrait printed in her own book: a slight young Black woman with a thoughtful, delicate face, in a plain dark dress with a white kerchief crossed at the neck, a white apron and a frilled white cap. She sits at a small round table with a sheet of paper before her, a quill in her right hand held just above the page, her left hand raised with one finger against her cheek, looking up and away as the next line comes to her. On the table are an inkstand, one candle and a small thick book lying open. The room is dark and bare behind her. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. Boston in the 1770s: no chains, no headwrap of a later period, no fine silk gown. Keep the top left corner darkness.
cards.check: Her age, the book of 1773 and the attestation (17 or 18 names) were confirmed. The search did not return the poem To Maecenas, which names Homer and Virgil.

cards.tx: Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: By his own account he was kidnapped as a boy from what is now Nigeria. Enslaved as a sailor, he traded on his own account until he had saved enough to buy his freedom, and his life story, published in 1789, helped to turn Britain against the slave trade.
cards.art: Olaudah Equiano on 11 July 1766, aged about twenty-one, on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, at the moment he becomes a free man: a young Black sailor with a broad, open face and short hair, in a sailor's short blue jacket, checked shirt and wide trousers, standing in a merchant's counting room with a sheet of paper, his freedom, held in both hands close to his chest. He has just been handed it; his eyes are shut and his head is thrown back, and he is drawing an enormous breath. On the desk in front of him lies the heap of coins he has paid, forty pounds, and behind the desk his former owner, a Quaker merchant in a plain brown coat and broad hat, is still holding the pen. A ship's captain claps Equiano on the shoulder. Through the door, the harbour and a sloop at anchor. Seen from the doorway, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No chains or whips in the picture, no bare-chested figure. Keep the top left corner plain wooden wall.
cards.check: Some scholars doubt his African birth; the card says it is his own account.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when she arrives.
cards.fact: She wrote her six novels of love, money and family on small sheets at a little table in the sitting room, and published them without her name; the title page of the first said only “By a Lady”. They have never been out of print.
cards.art: Jane Austen about 1813, aged thirty-seven, writing in the dining parlour of her cottage at Chawton: a slim woman with a round face, bright hazel eyes, a small firm mouth and dark curls showing at the front of a white muslin cap, in a plain high-waisted dress with long sleeves. She sits by the window at a very small round walnut table, hardly bigger than a dinner plate, writing on small sheets of paper with a quill. The door of the room, behind her, has begun to open with a creak, and without turning her head she is sliding a sheet of blotting paper over the page with her left hand, her eyes going sideways toward the door and the corner of her mouth lifting. A work basket, a teapot, a garden beyond the glass. Seen from across the little table, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. England in 1813: no bonnet indoors, no wide Victorian skirts, no typewriter. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.tx: At the end of a round, if you hold his Place, draw a card.
cards.fact: He could not read any language, yet over about twelve years he worked out 86 signs, one for each syllable of Cherokee. Within a few years most of his people could read and write, and they had their own newspaper.
cards.art: Sequoyah in 1821, showing the leaders of the Cherokee Nation that his signs can carry speech, with the help of his young daughter Ayoka: a man of about fifty with a calm, deep-lined face, dressed as the portrait painted of him in 1828 shows him, in a blue coat over a white shirt, a red cloth wound around his head as a turban, a long-stemmed pipe in his hand, sitting on a bench with his lame leg stretched out. He watches without a word as his daughter, a girl of about six in a calico dress, who was sent out of the room while the men told him what to write, stands in the doorway and reads their message aloud from a sheet of paper covered in his characters. The headmen, in turbans, hunting coats and trade-cloth shirts, lean toward her, one with his hand over his mouth. A log council house, a low fire. Seen from beside the girl, so that Sequoyah faces us from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No feathered headdress, no tipi, no buckskin fringe costume. Keep the top left corner log wall.

links.hokusai>hiroshige: Hiroshige turned to landscape after Hokusai's views of Mount Fuji had made such prints the fashion in Edo.

cards.tx: Legacy of Hokusai.
cards.fact: The son of a fire warden, he kept his own post in the Edo fire brigade for years while he learned to draw. His prints of travellers caught in rain, snow and mist on the road to Kyoto sold in the thousands.
cards.art: Hiroshige in 1832, aged thirty-five, sketching on the great road from Edo to Kyoto as a sudden summer storm breaks: a round-faced, mild-looking man with a shaved crown and a small topknot, in a travelling kimono tucked up at the knees with leggings and straw sandals, sitting on the bench of a roadside tea stall under its dripping thatched eave. A small sketchbook is open on his knee and his brush is moving fast, but his eyes are on the road, where two bearers with a covered litter and a man hunched under a paper umbrella are running bent double up a hill into slanting grey rain, while a grove of bamboo behind them bows in the wind in three fading bands of grey. The tea woman holds out a cup he has not noticed. Seen from the road, looking in under the eave, Hiroshige from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Edo Japan: no great wave, no Mount Fuji, no samurai armour. Keep the top left corner thatch and rain.

links.shakespeare>goethe: Goethe wrote that the first page of Shakespeare he read made him Shakespeare's for life.

cards.tx: Legacy of Shakespeare. Scholar.
cards.fact: Poet, playwright, minister of a small German state and student of plants and colours, he worked on his great play Faust, about a scholar who bargains with the devil, for some sixty years. He finished it only months before he died.
cards.art: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in April 1787, aged thirty-seven, in the public garden at Palermo in Sicily, where the idea came to him that all plants are variations on one plan: a tall, handsome man with large dark eyes, a strong nose and his brown hair tied back unpowdered, in a pale travelling coat, with a broad-brimmed grey hat lying on the path beside him. He has gone down on one knee in front of a bed of strange southern plants and holds a single large leaf flat on his palm, tracing its ribs with a pencil, while a pocket volume of Homer, which he came out to read, lies forgotten face down in the grass. Lemon trees, palms and tall flowering stems surround him, and the sea is blue beyond a wall. Seen from the flower bed, low, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Italy in 1787: no powdered wig, no devil or scholar's study, no reclining pose among ruins. Keep the top left corner palm fronds.
cards.check: The sixty years on Faust, finished in 1831, were confirmed. The search did not return his words about Shakespeare (the speech Zum Shakespeares-Tag, 1771).

cards.tx: She can't be clashed.
cards.fact: She seldom left her family's house, and in later years spoke to visitors from behind a half-open door. Only about ten of her poems were printed while she lived; after she died her sister found nearly eighteen hundred, many sewn by hand into little books.
cards.art: Emily Dickinson about 1865, aged thirty-five, at the upstairs window of her family's brick house in Amherst, lowering a treat to the children of the neighbourhood: a small, slight woman with auburn hair parted in the middle and drawn back, dark eyes and a quick, shy smile, in a plain white cotton dress with a row of buttons down the front. She leans out over the sill with both hands paying out a cord, at the end of which a little basket of gingerbread swings down past the shutters toward three children who stand in the garden below with their arms stretched up, only the tops of their heads and their hands in the picture. Behind her in the room is a small square writing table with a lamp and a few folded papers. Summer leaves frame the window. Seen from outside and a little below, Emily from the waist up in the window, her face in the upper right. New England in the 1860s: no black dress, no veil, no gravestones. Keep the top left corner brick wall and leaves.
cards.check: The half-open door and the basket of gingerbread were not returned.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: A count who had fought as an army officer, he wrote War and Peace, a novel with more than five hundred characters. In old age he dressed as a peasant, worked in the fields and taught that nobody should answer violence with violence.
cards.art: Leo Tolstoy about 1890, aged sixty-two, mowing hay with the peasants on his own estate: a big, strong old man with a long grey-white beard, shaggy brows and small piercing eyes, in a loose white peasant blouse belted at the waist, rough trousers tucked into boots and a soft cap. He swings a long-handled scythe in the middle of a line of mowers who move in step across a meadow at sunrise, the grass falling in a curved swath at his feet, sweat darkening his shirt, his face set and content. The men on either side of him are younger and bearded, in the same dress, and one glances at him to see whether the old count can keep the pace. Women rake behind; a white manor house shows through birch trees far off. Seen from in front of the line, low, Tolstoy from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Russia in the 1890s: no officer's uniform, no writing desk, no fur coat. Keep the top left corner dawn sky.
cards.check: Not searched for his own facts (the Gandhi letters and Tolstoy Farm were confirmed under Gandhi).

links.mozart>tchaikovsky: Tchaikovsky loved Mozart above all other composers, and built his suite Mozartiana from Mozart's tunes.

cards.tx: Legacy of Mozart.
cards.fact: He trained as a law clerk before he gave himself to music. His ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker are danced all over the world, though Swan Lake was coldly received when it was first staged.
cards.art: Pyotr Tchaikovsky in February 1877, aged thirty-six, at a rehearsal of his first ballet in the great theatre in Moscow: a neat, anxious man with a short dark beard, a high forehead and gentle eyes, in a dark frock coat, sitting alone in the empty front rows of the stalls with the big handwritten score open across his knees and a pencil between his teeth, both hands gripping the seat in front of him. On the stage above, in the hard light of the gas footlights, a line of dancers in white knee-length skirts of gauze with small wings at the shoulders holds a pose against a painted lake and a painted moon, and the ballet master is waving his stick at them in a temper. The gilded tiers of boxes rise empty into the dark. Seen from the orchestra rail, looking back at him, Tchaikovsky from the waist up, his face in the upper right, the dancers reflected small in the lower left. Russia in 1877: no short stiff modern tutu, no grey-haired old man. Keep the top left corner dark boxes.
cards.check: The law school, the clerk's post and the cold reception of Swan Lake in 1877 were confirmed. The search did not return Mozartiana.

cards.tx: On arrival, gain 1 Spark, or 2 if the other player holds this Place.
cards.fact: Samuel Clemens took his pen name from the cry of the Mississippi riverboat men, “mark twain”, which means water two fathoms deep and safe to steam through. He was born in a year when Halley's Comet passed, said he expected to go out with it, and died the day after it came closest to the Sun again.
cards.art: Samuel Clemens, later Mark Twain, in 1859, aged twenty-three, a newly licensed pilot on a Mississippi steamboat: a slim young man with a thick mop of reddish-brown curls, bushy brows over sharp grey-green eyes and side whiskers, in a blue pilot's jacket with brass buttons over a white shirt.
