He stands high in the glass-sided pilot house at an enormous wooden steering wheel, taller than he is and half sunk through the floor, with both hands on its spokes and his whole body leaning into the turn, his eyes narrowed on the brown river ahead where a line of ripples marks a sandbar at a bend. A speaking tube and a bell pull hang beside him, and the tall black smokestacks of the boat rise outside the glass. Far below on the foredeck a man is swinging a sounding line. Dawn mist on the water. Seen from the back of the pilot house, a little to one side, from the knees up, his face in three-quarter view in the upper right. No white suit, no white hair or moustache, no cigar. Keep the top left corner window frame and mist.

links.hiroshige>vangogh: Van Gogh collected Japanese prints, and in 1887 he copied two of Hiroshige's in oil paint to learn from them.

cards.tx: Legacy of Hiroshige. Swift: he can walk on the turn he arrives.
cards.fact: He took up painting at twenty-seven and made nearly nine hundred paintings in the ten years he had left, at times one a day. He sold very few, and never knew that they would be among the best loved in the world.
cards.art: Vincent van Gogh in September 1888, aged thirty-five, painting the stars over the river Rhône at Arles, out of doors at night, as he wrote that he did: a wiry man with cropped red hair, a red beard and pale, burning eyes, in a blue workman's jacket and a battered felt hat, standing on the stone quay at a folding easel set under a street gas lamp. He holds a loaded brush out at arm's length toward the sky, measuring, and a palette thick with paint is hooked on his other thumb. Beyond him the dark river carries long trembling reflections of the town's yellow gaslights, and overhead the stars of the Great Bear hang large in a deep blue-green sky. A couple strolls on the bank below. Seen from along the quay, from the knees up, his face lit from above in the upper right. No candles on his hat, no bandaged ear, no sunflowers, and his canvas is turned away so that the painting itself is not shown. Keep the top left corner night sky.
cards.check: His age when he began and the count of paintings were not returned.

cards.tx: Swift: he can walk on the turn he arrives.
cards.fact: His Maple Leaf Rag of 1899 sold hundreds of thousands of copies as sheet music and paid him a penny on every one. He was called the King of Ragtime, and more than seventy years later his tune The Entertainer was a hit all over again.
cards.art: Scott Joplin in the late summer of 1899, aged about thirty-one, in a music shop in Sedalia, Missouri, on the day his Maple Leaf Rag is first in print: a slight, quiet, serious young Black man with close-cut hair and a clean-shaven face, in a neat dark three-piece suit with a high white collar and a tie, standing at the shop counter. He has taken the top copy from a fresh stack of sheet music and holds it open in both hands, reading down the page, his lips pressed together and the fingers of his right hand, without his knowing it, tapping the rhythm on the edge of the paper. The white-bearded shop owner watches him over his spectacles from behind the counter. Violins and banjos hang on the wall and an upright piano stands closed in the corner. Seen from the shop door, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Missouri in 1899: nobody is playing, no straw boater and striped jacket, no saloon. Keep the top left corner shelves in shadow.
cards.check: Sources say the rag sold more than a million copies in the end.

cards.tx: Steadfast: she has +2 Might when she defends.
cards.fact: A bus crash at eighteen broke her spine and left her in pain for the rest of her life. She began to paint lying in bed, with a mirror fixed above her, and about a third of all her pictures are portraits of herself.
cards.art: Frida Kahlo in 1926, aged nineteen, a year after the accident, painting in bed at her family's blue house in Coyoacán: a young woman with strong dark brows that almost meet, black hair parted in the middle and pinned back, and a level, unflinching gaze, propped on pillows in a wooden four-poster bed. Her body is held rigid from hips to armpits in a white plaster corset under an embroidered blouse. A small wooden easel made for her stands across her lap with a canvas on it, its back to us, and she holds a fine brush in her right hand and a little palette in her left, but she is not looking at the canvas: she is looking up, into a mirror fixed to the underside of the bed's canopy, in which we see her face again, small and upside down. Paint tubes on the blanket, a window on a courtyard with a lemon tree. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face in the upper right and the mirror above her at the top centre. No monkey, no flower crown, no skeletons. Keep the top left corner plain canopy cloth.
cards.check: The count of 55 self-portraits among 143 paintings was found in one weak source only.

cards.tx: He can't be clashed.
cards.fact: He became pharaoh at about nine and died at about nineteen. His small tomb lay hidden under the huts of later tomb builders for more than three thousand years, and when it was opened in 1922 it still held over five thousand objects, among them a mask of solid gold.
cards.art: Tutankhamun about 1325 BC, aged about seventeen, in a palace garden with his young queen, drawn after the scenes on the furniture from his own tomb: a slender youth with a narrow face and large almond eyes, in a long pleated kilt of fine white linen with a wide sash, a broad collar of coloured beads on his bare chest, sandals, and a close blue crown with a gold cobra at the brow. He leans with both hands on a tall walking stick, one foot set a little behind the other, as scenes from his tomb show him, and bends his head toward the queen, who stands facing him in a clinging pleated dress and a heavy wig and holds up to him two bunches of lotus and papyrus flowers. Behind them are a pool with ducks, fruit trees and a painted pavilion. Composed in the soft, natural style of the art of his own short reign. Seen from the side, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No gold mask on his face, no mummy, no curse. Keep the top left corner leaves and sky.
cards.check: His ages were not returned. Whether he was lame is disputed, so the brief shows the stick without saying why.

cards.tx: He can't be moved. He has +1 Might for each round he stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: He ruled Egypt for sixty-six years, fathered about a hundred children and built on a grander scale than any pharaoh before or after. At Abu Simbel he had a temple cut into a cliff so that twice a year the rising Sun reaches the statues at its very back.
cards.art: Ramesses II about 1250 BC, in his fifties, inside his rock temple at Abu Simbel at the moment of sunrise on one of the two days of the year when the light reaches its heart: a tall, lean pharaoh with a high-bridged, hooked nose and a long jaw, in a pleated linen robe with wide sleeves, a broad jewelled collar and the tall blue war crown with a gold cobra, holding up a small bowl of burning incense in both hands. He stands in the dark inner chamber, and a single level beam of gold light, come all the way down the long hall behind us, strikes his raised arms and face and the knees of four seated stone figures against the back wall behind him, of which three are lit and the one at the left end stays in shadow. Painted reliefs glimmer on the side walls. Seen from the hall, looking in along the beam, the king from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No pyramids, no striped headcloth, no mummy. Keep the top left corner darkness.
cards.check: Counts of his children run from 88 to 103.

cards.cap: Samos and Croton, c. 570 to c. 495 BC
cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: He led a secretive brotherhood in southern Italy who lived by strict rules, kept away from meat, and believed that number is the key to everything. They found that strings whose lengths stand as two to one, or three to two, sound sweet together.
cards.art: Pythagoras about 520 BC at Croton in southern Italy, showing his followers that music is number: a tall, grave man of about fifty with long hair and a full dark beard streaked with grey, in a long white linen robe, standing in a courtyard at dusk. He holds across his body a plain sounding box of wood with a single gut string stretched along it, and with one finger he presses a small movable bridge exactly at the middle of the string while his other hand plucks one half; his head is bent to the sound. A half circle of men and women, all in white, sits on the ground before him in silence, some with their eyes closed, and one young man holds a knotted cord marked off in equal parts. The first stars are out above the wall. Seen from among the listeners, Pythagoras from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Greek Italy in the sixth century BC: no triangle diagram held up like a sign, no telescope, no lyre with many strings. Keep the top left corner dusk sky.

cards.tx: He can't be moved. He has +1 Might for each round he stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: He became king of the Maya city of Palenque at twelve and ruled for sixty-eight years, one of the longest reigns in history. In 1952 his tomb was found deep inside a pyramid, his face covered with a mask of jade.
cards.art: Pakal of Palenque on the day in the year 615 when he becomes king at twelve years old, drawn after the carved stone panel in his own palace that shows the scene: a slim boy with the long sloping forehead and high-bridged nose the Maya admired, his hair cut in steps and tied up in a plume, wearing a short kilt, a wide collar and wristbands of green jade beads. He sits cross-legged on a low throne carved as a jaguar with a head at each end, turned toward his mother, who kneels before him in a net-patterned dress and cape and lifts up to him in both hands a tall crown made of small plates of jade and shell. He reaches for it gravely with one hand. Behind them are the white plastered walls of a palace room painted with red bands, and through a doorway the roof combs of temples stand above the forest in mist. Seen from the side, Pakal from the waist up, his face in the upper right. The Maya of the seventh century: no Aztec sun stone, no feather war bonnet, no sacrifice. Keep the top left corner plain plaster wall.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when she arrives.
cards.fact: An abbess on the Rhine, she wrote down the visions she had seen since childhood, along with books about medicine and plants. More of her music survives than of any other composer of her time, some seventy songs with their words and their tunes.
cards.art: Hildegard of Bingen about 1150, aged fifty-two, receiving a vision and writing it down, drawn after the picture at the front of her own book: a woman with a pale, strong face lifted upward and wide grey eyes, in the black habit and veil of a Benedictine nun, seated on a wooden chair in a small arched cell. From a square opening in the roof above her five long tongues of red and gold flame reach down and touch her forehead, and she, without looking at her hands, is writing with a pointed stylus on a pair of hinged wax tablets held on her knee. At the right edge a tonsured monk, her secretary, has put his head through a little window in the cell wall and stares up at the flames, a sheet of parchment forgotten in his hand. Composed with the flat colour and gold ground of a twelfth-century manuscript painting. Seen from inside the cell, from the waist up, her face in the upper half, right of centre. No halo, no harp, no witch's herbs. Keep the top left corner plain painted arch.

cards.tx: He can't be moved. He has +1 Might for each round he stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: King of Ethiopia, he is remembered for eleven churches at his capital that were not built up from the ground but carved down into it, each cut from the solid rock. Pilgrims still come to pray in them, and the town now bears his name.
cards.art: Lalibela, king of Ethiopia, about the year 1200, at the rim of the pit in which one of his churches is being carved downward out of the living rock: a lean, dark, bearded man of middle age with a calm, absorbed face, in long white cotton robes with a coloured border, a white cloth wound around his head beneath a plain gold band, holding a tall staff topped with a cross. He stands at the very edge of a deep square trench cut in a hillside of red-brown stone and looks down into it. Below him, at the bottom of the picture, the flat roof of the church is already finished, a great cross within a cross carved in the rock, level with the ground, and far down around its walls tiny masons on ladders are hollowing out windows and doors with iron picks and carrying away baskets of chips. Priests in white stand behind the king with a drum and a book. Seen from across the trench, the king from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No angels shown, no European crown, no built stonework of blocks. Keep the top left corner dry hillside and sky.
cards.check: Tradition gives all eleven churches to his reign; some scholars think the work ran longer.

links.elizabeth>grace: Grace O'Malley sailed to England in 1593 and put her case to Queen Elizabeth face to face.

cards.cap: Clew Bay, Ireland, c. 1530 to c. 1603
cards.tx: Voyager. Raider: she has +2 Might when she attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: Chieftain of a seafaring clan on the west coast of Ireland, she commanded her own fleet of galleys for decades, and the English called her a pirate. At about sixty-three she sailed to London and argued her case before Queen Elizabeth, who granted most of what she asked.
cards.art: Grace O'Malley, Gráinne Ní Mháille, about 1577, at her tower house on the shore of Clew Bay in the west of Ireland, sending her galleys to sea: a tall, weathered woman in her late forties with grey-streaked dark hair blowing loose and a hard, humorous face, in the dress of a Gaelic noblewoman, a full-sleeved linen tunic dyed yellow under a heavy fringed wool mantle fastened at the breast, a long knife at her belt. She stands at the head of the sea steps under a plain square stone tower, one hand on the wet rock, the other pointing out to the mouth of the bay, calling an order down to the nearer of two long, low ships with a single mast and a row of oars on each side, whose crews are pushing off. A mooring rope runs from the ship up through a slit window of the tower above her. Islands, rain cloud and a gap of bright sea. Seen from the water below the steps, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Sixteenth-century Ireland: no eyepatch, no three-cornered hat, no skull flag, no cannon broadside. Keep the top left corner tower wall and cloud.
cards.check: Accounts differ on whether she and the queen spoke in Latin or English; the card does not say.

cards.tx: On arrival, gain 2 Spark.
cards.fact: When his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, the emperor of India set some twenty thousand workers to build her a tomb of white marble, the Taj Mahal. He spent his last eight years a prisoner of his own son, in a fort from which he could see it across the river.
cards.art: Shah Jahan about 1665, in his seventies, a prisoner in the fort at Agra, looking across the river at the tomb he built for his wife: a thin, upright old man with a long white beard and a fine, sad face, in a plain white muslin coat tied at the side and a small turban with a single pearl, seated on a cushion in an eight-sided marble pavilion whose walls are inlaid with flowers of coloured stone. He sits turned away from the room, one hand on the carved marble screen of the balcony, gazing out. Beyond the screen the wide river bends away in the haze of early morning, and on its far bank, small and pale and perfect, stand the white dome and four slim towers of the Taj Mahal. His eldest daughter sits behind him with a book. Seen from inside the pavilion, a little to one side, the emperor from the waist up, his face in profile in the upper right, the tomb in the distance at the centre left. Mughal India: no jewelled throne, no courtiers, no sword. Keep the top left corner inlaid marble wall.

links.wollstonecraft>shelley: Mary Shelley was Mary Wollstonecraft's daughter. Her mother died days after she was born, and she grew up reading her books.

cards.tx: Legacy of Mary Wollstonecraft. Scholar.
cards.fact: Kept indoors by storms at a house on Lake Geneva in the cold summer of 1816, she and her friends agreed that each would write a ghost story. She was eighteen, and hers became Frankenstein, the tale of a student who builds a living man and runs from what he has made.
cards.art: Mary Godwin, soon to be Mary Shelley, in June 1816, aged eighteen, on the stormy night at a villa above Lake Geneva when the idea of Frankenstein comes to her: a slight, fair girl with a high clear forehead, hazel eyes and light brown hair parted in the middle, in a plain high-waisted dress with a shawl. She stands alone at a tall window with one hand pressed flat to the glass and a candle in the other, and she has gone rigid, staring not at the lake but at something in her own mind; a fork of lightning over the black water and the far mountains lights her face white. Behind her in the room three young men talk by the fire, careless shapes in firelight with books and wine glasses, and none of them has noticed her. Rain on the panes. Seen from outside the window looking in, Mary from the waist up, her face in the upper right. 1816: no monster shown anywhere, no laboratory, no bolts, no castle. Keep the top left corner dark window frame and rain.

cards.tx: At the end of a round, if you hold his Place, draw a card.
cards.fact: A poor shoemaker's son, he left home alone at fourteen to seek his fortune in Copenhagen. He wrote more than 150 fairy tales, among them The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling and The Emperor's New Clothes, and he could cut whole scenes out of folded paper while he told them.
cards.art: Hans Christian Andersen about 1850, aged forty-five, telling a story to the children of a Danish country house and cutting it out of paper as he goes: a very tall, thin, awkward man with a long nose, deep-set small eyes and a kind, mobile face, in a black frock coat with a high collar and a loose silk tie, perched on a chair too low for him with his knees up. In his big hands are a pair of enormous paper scissors and a folded sheet of white paper, from which he is just drawing apart, like a concertina, a long chain of joined figures: a row of dancers, a swan at each end, a little man in a tall hat. Four children press around his knees, one already holding an earlier cutting up to the window so that the daylight shines through it. A tiled stove, a rag rug. Seen from behind the smallest child, Andersen from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Denmark about 1850: no mermaid or duckling drawn in the room, no wizard's robe. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.tx: On arrival, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He wrote poems and tales of dread, among them The Raven, and in 1841 he invented the detective story, with a hero who solves a murder by reasoning alone. He was found dying in Baltimore at forty, and nobody has ever explained what had happened to him.
cards.art: Edgar Allan Poe in the winter of 1846, aged thirty-seven, writing by night in his small cottage outside New York: a slight man with a very broad pale forehead, dark tumbled hair, a dark moustache and large, shadowed grey eyes, in a worn black coat buttoned to the neck against the cold. He sits at a bare table writing with a steel pen on a long narrow strip of paper made of sheets pasted end to end, which trails off the table and curls on the floor. A large tortoiseshell cat sits upright on his shoulder, as she really did, watching the pen. One candle; its light throws his shadow and the cat's, joined into a single strange tall shape, up the whitewashed wall behind him. A cold hearth and a few books on a hanging shelf. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No raven, no skull, no bottle. Keep the top left corner bare wall above the shadow.
cards.check: The cat on his shoulder and the strips of pasted paper are in the picture brief only and were not returned.

links.poe>verne: Jules Verne admired Edgar Allan Poe's tales, and wrote a sequel to Poe's story of a voyage toward the South Pole.

cards.tx: Legacy of Edgar Allan Poe. Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Before a submarine had crossed an ocean or anyone had left the ground in an aeroplane, he sent his heroes under the sea, around the Moon and around the world in eighty days, working out each journey with the science and the timetables of his day. He is one of the most translated authors there has ever been.
cards.art: Jules Verne about 1870, aged forty-two, writing in the tiny cabin of his own sailing boat on the coast of northern France, where he wrote much of his tale of a voyage under the sea: a broad-shouldered man with curly brown hair, a full beard and lively pale eyes, in a seaman's knitted jersey and a pea jacket, sitting wedged on a narrow bunk at a fold-down table that slopes with the boat. He writes in pencil in a thick notebook, steadying an inkwell with his elbow, and has looked up at the round brass-rimmed window beside his head, against which a green wave has just broken, so that for a moment the glass is full of water and light, as if the boat were under the sea. A sea chart, a lamp swinging on its hook, a row of scientific journals behind a rail. Seen from the cabin door, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. France about 1870: no submarine, no diving helmet, no balloon. Keep the top left corner dark deck beams.
cards.check: That he is among the most translated authors was not returned.

links.sittingbull>oakley: Sitting Bull saw Annie Oakley shoot in 1884, adopted her as a daughter, and gave her a name that means Little Sure Shot.

cards.tx: She has +2 Might when she attacks a stronger Figure.
cards.fact: She learned to shoot as a child to feed her family, and at fifteen she out-shot a travelling marksman, whom she later married. In Buffalo Bill's show she could hit the thin edge of a playing card at thirty paces.
cards.art: Annie Oakley about 1888, aged twenty-eight, in the arena of the Wild West show, making her most famous shot: a very small, neat woman with long dark hair down her back and a calm, intent face, in the costume she sewed herself, a calf-length skirt and a fitted jacket with a line of fringe, leggings, and a wide-brimmed hat pinned up at one side with a star, a row of shooting medals on her chest. She stands with her back to her target, a rifle laid over her right shoulder pointing behind her, and aims by looking into a small hand mirror that she holds up in her left hand; in the mirror we can just see the tiny reflection of a man far across the arena holding out a playing card edge-on. Her face is all concentration, one eye closed. Canvas tents, a grandstand full of hats. Seen from in front of her, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. No feathers, no short skirt, no two pistols twirling. Correct anatomy, two hands. Keep the top left corner tent canvas and sky.
cards.check: The playing card and the mirror shot were not returned. Sitting Bull's adoption of her was informal.

cards.tx: Swift. He can't be clashed.
cards.fact: Born Erik Weisz in Budapest, he could slip out of handcuffs, chains, jail cells and a locked tank of water in which he hung upside down. He also spent years exposing fake mediums who claimed to speak with the dead.
cards.art: Harry Houdini about 1916, aged forty-two, hanging head down in a straitjacket high above a city street: a short, very muscular man with curly dark hair standing out from his head and a face clenched with effort, his ankles bound in a padded harness to a rope that runs up to a beam jutting from the top of a tall newspaper building. He is strapped into a canvas straitjacket with leather buckles, his arms crossed and pinned, and he is doubled up at the waist, twisting, with one shoulder already worked half free. He fills the upper part of the picture, upside down, and far beneath him the whole street from wall to wall is a sea of upturned faces and straw hats, with stopped trams and people leaning from every window. Seen from a window level with him, his whole figure in the upper half, his face right of centre and the right way round enough to read. No chains, no water tank, no top hat or wand. Correct anatomy. Keep the top left corner sky and the edge of the building.

cards.tx: Voyager: she can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: In 1932 she became the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic, landing in a farmer's field in Northern Ireland after nearly fifteen hours in the air. Five years later she vanished over the Pacific on a flight around the world, and no trace of her aeroplane has been confirmed.
cards.art: Amelia Earhart on 21 May 1932, aged thirty-four, minutes after landing alone from across the Atlantic in a cow pasture in the north of Ireland: a tall, slim woman with a freckled, wind-burned face, grey eyes and short tousled fair hair, in a leather flying jacket over a checked shirt, riding breeches and laced boots, a silk scarf at her neck. She is climbing out through the hatch in the roof of a bright red single-engined aeroplane with a high wing and a round nose, one leg over the edge, pulling off her leather helmet with one hand and laughing down, tired out, at a farm labourer in a flat cap who has run up and is staring at her with a hay fork still in his hand. Cows stand off at a distance. Wet green hills, stone walls, low cloud. Seen from the grass beside the labourer, Earhart from the knees up, her face in the upper right. No goggles over her eyes, no second person in the aeroplane, no ocean liner. Keep the top left corner cloud.
cards.check: The landing was at Culmore, near Derry.

links.hypatia>astrolabe: Hypatia's father Theon wrote a book on the astrolabe that later writers built on, and one of her students thanked her for teaching him how to make one.

cards.cap: Alexandria and Baghdad, from the 4th century
cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A traveller who can read the sky knows the way.
cards.fact: With one brass disc a traveller could tell the time by the Sun or a star, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of a tower. An astronomer of the tenth century described about a thousand uses for it.
cards.art: A brass astrolabe of the Islamic world, about the tenth century, hanging from a hand by the ring at its top against a clear night sky: a flat round instrument a little wider than the hand that holds it, its face an openwork plate of curling pointers, each one marking a star, laid over a disc engraved with fine arcs and circles, with a straight sighting bar pinned across the back. It turns slightly on its ring and catches lamplight. Behind it, out of focus, are the flat roofs and one dome of a city and a field of real stars that the pointers echo. Only the hand and wrist of the holder are in the picture, in a plain wide sleeve. Historically accurate: no glass, no magnetic needle, no numbers or letters that can be read. The instrument is in the upper half, right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: Theon's book was not the earliest on the astrolabe.

links.cailun>paper: Cai Lun showed the Han court in 105 how to make good paper from bark, hemp, rags and old nets.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Cheap pages meant more books for more readers.
cards.fact: For centuries only China knew how to make it. Paper reached Samarkand in the 700s and Baghdad before the year 800, and Spain about two hundred years after that, and wherever it arrived, books became cheaper.
cards.art: Newly made sheets of paper drying in the sun in a Chinese papermaker's yard of about the second century: a long whitewashed wall with a dozen pale, slightly rough-edged sheets pressed flat against it, the nearest one beginning to curl away at one corner in the breeze, its fibres catching the light. In front of the wall stand a wooden vat of grey pulp with a cloth-covered frame resting across it, a stone mortar, and a basket of bark strips, rags and a tangle of old fishing net. A single finished sheet lies on a low table under a brush and an ink stone, still blank. No people. Historically accurate: no printed or written characters anywhere, no bound books, no scrolls on rollers. The drying sheets fill the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain plain wall and sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: paper was in Muslim Spain by the 900s.

links.napoleon>rosetta: Soldiers of the army Napoleon took to Egypt found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, built into an old wall they were pulling down.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: One stone opened three thousand years of writing.
cards.fact: The same decree is carved on it three times: in hieroglyphs, in the everyday script of Egypt and in Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, and that was their way in to the other two.
cards.art: The Rosetta Stone as it was found in July 1799, half dug out of the rubble of an old fort wall in the Nile delta: a slab of dark grey stone about as tall as a child of ten, its top corners and one lower corner broken away, standing tilted in a trench of sand and broken brick. Its polished face is covered from top to bottom with fine carved writing in three bands that are plainly different from each other: small pictures at the top, a flowing script in the middle, and neat square letters at the bottom. A soldier's pick and a wooden measuring rod lean beside it, and a hand has just brushed the dust from the middle band. Hard sunlight rakes across the carving. No people but the one hand. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no gold, no pyramids behind. The stone stands in the upper half, right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and wall.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: Thirty miles in an hour, where a horse did thirty in a day.
cards.fact: At trials near Liverpool in 1829 a locomotive named Rocket ran at about thirty miles an hour, a speed no horse could keep up for long. Within twenty years Britain had laid some six thousand miles of railway.
cards.art: The locomotive Rocket at speed in October 1829: a small engine painted bright yellow with black bands, with a tall thin white chimney at the front, a short barrel of a boiler, two big spoked driving wheels turned by cylinders set at a slant on each side, and a pair of small wheels behind, pulling a four-wheeled tender that carries a water barrel. It rushes from left to right along a plain iron track on a low embankment, white steam streaming back flat from the chimney, the driver and fireman small dark figures on the footplate, one holding his hat on. A marquee with two flags stands far back; nobody else is in the picture. Seen from the trackside, low, the engine in the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no cab roof, no cowcatcher, no headlamp, no later streamlining. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and steam.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: It lifted people over everything that stood in their way.
cards.fact: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon, sent up before the king of France in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Two months later two men flew across Paris for about twenty-five minutes, feeding a fire of straw beneath the paper-lined bag as they went.
cards.art: The balloon of the Montgolfier brothers on 21 November 1783, floating over the roofs of Paris with the first two people ever to fly: a huge pear-shaped bag of cloth and paper painted deep blue and gold, decorated with suns, swags of drapery and the signs of the zodiac, taller than a church. Around its open neck runs a narrow wicker gallery, and in it, on opposite sides to balance it, stand two tiny men in coats and hats, one waving his hat and the other pushing a forkful of straw into an iron fire basket that hangs in the opening. A thread of smoke trails away. Below lie grey slate roofs, church towers and the river with its bridges, and on one near roof three people, each different, looking up. Seen from the air a little below the balloon, which fills the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no gas burner, no hanging basket on ropes, no modern bright stripes. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain clear sky.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: It lifted a person over everything that stood in the way.
cards.fact: On 17 December 1903 two bicycle makers from Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright, made the first flights in a powered aeroplane. The first lasted twelve seconds and covered less ground than the wingspan of a modern airliner.
cards.art: The Wright brothers' aeroplane on the morning of 17 December 1903 at the instant it leaves the ground: a frail machine of spruce and pale cloth with two long wings one above the other, a pair of small flat surfaces held out in front on struts, a double rudder behind, and two slow wooden propellers at the back driven by chains. It has just lifted a hand's breadth off the end of a single wooden rail laid on flat sand. One man lies face down on the lower wing with his hips in a cradle and his hands on a lever; the other, in a dark suit and cap, has let go of the wing tip and stands frozen in mid-stride, watching. A low bench and a coil of wire lie on the sand. Cold grey light, wind off the sea, a big dune behind. Seen from behind and to the right, the machine in the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no wheels, no seat, no enclosed body, no engine cowling. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain blank winter sky.
cards.check: The flights were at Kill Devil Hills, four miles from Kitty Hawk.

links.arminius>teutoburg: Arminius led three Roman legions into the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 and destroyed them there.

cards.tx: One of your Figures clashes with an enemy at its Place with +1 Might, even if it has already acted.
cards.fit: A whole army was struck from behind a wall when it could not form up.
cards.fact: In AD 9 three Roman legions were strung out along a narrow track between a wooded hill and a bog, in the rain, when Arminius's warriors struck from behind a wall of turf. Traces of that wall and thousands of lost Roman things have been dug up at Kalkriese in Germany.
cards.art: The ambush in the Teutoburg Forest in September of AD 9, seen from low on the track: a narrow, muddy path between a steep wooded slope on the left and a reedy bog on the right, in heavy rain. Along the foot of the slope runs a low wall of cut turf topped with wattle, and over it three Germanic warriors, each different in age and build, with long narrow shields and spears, are coming down onto the path. Facing them are three Roman soldiers, each different, caught out of order: one in a mail shirt still pulling the leather rain cover off his big curved shield, one dragging at a baggage mule, one turning with his short sword half drawn. In the mud at the lower right lies a Roman cavalryman's face mask of silvered iron, fallen and staring up, rain beading on it. The rest of both armies is hidden by rain and trees. No horned or winged helmets, no close view of wounds, no rows or columns of repeated figures. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wet branches.

links.caesar>testudo: In his own account of invading Britain, Caesar tells how the Seventh Legion locked shields into a tortoise to storm a stronghold in the woods.

cards.tx: Quick. One of your Figures gets +2 Might for one clash. On the other player's turn it plays itself when it would save your Figure, paid for with 1 Spark you kept.
cards.fit: Locked shields carried soldiers through what would have stopped them.
cards.fact: Testudo is Latin for tortoise. Roman soldiers locked their shields edge to edge in front, at the sides and over their heads, and walked up to an enemy wall under a rain of arrows and stones.
cards.art: A Roman tortoise of shields about 54 BC, seen from the wall it is attacking, looking down: a tight block of some thirty soldiers has become a single roof of long oval shields, overlapping like tiles, with a wall of shields along the front and sides and only sandalled feet and the tips of a few short swords showing at the edges. Stones and javelins thrown from above are bouncing off the shield roof, one in mid-air, and a clay pot has just smashed across it. The block moves steadily up a ramp of piled brushwood toward us. Nobody else is in the picture: the formation is the subject, small enough to be seen whole. Every shield carries the same painted pattern. Seen from above and in front, the formation in the middle and upper half of the picture. The late Roman Republic: oval shields curved like a section of barrel, mail shirts, plain bronze helmets; no rectangular shields, no segmented plate. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain earth bank and sky.
cards.check: Caesar, Gallic War 5.9.

links.douglass>brownsbox: Frederick Douglass wished Henry Brown's escape in a box had been kept quiet, so that others could have got away by the same road.

cards.tx: A Figure costing 3 or less arrives from your hand at any Place.
cards.fit: He arrived where nobody could stop him, shut inside a box.
cards.fact: In 1849 Henry Brown, enslaved in Virginia, had himself nailed into a wooden box about three feet long and sent by express to Philadelphia. He travelled twenty-seven hours by wagon, train and steamboat, part of the way upside down, and stepped out a free man.
cards.art: Henry Brown's box on its way north in March 1849: a plain crate of rough boards, about three feet long and two wide, bound with five hoops of hickory, standing among trunks, mail sacks and barrels in the dim baggage car of a moving train. A paper label is pasted on its lid, and three small holes are bored in one end. Two railway porters in caps and aprons are sitting on it, one at each end, sharing a pipe, with no idea what is under them. A swinging lantern lights the car; through the half-open sliding door the night country streams past. In one of the three small holes, if one looks closely, a little lamplight catches the white of an eye. Seen from across the car, the crate in the middle of the picture and the porters' heads in the upper half. Historically accurate: no bars, no chains, no lettering that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark roof of the car.
cards.check: That he travelled part of the way upside down was not returned.

links.darwin>beagle: Charles Darwin sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle, and filled the ship with the rocks, bones and animals he collected.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: Five years of collecting came home in one small ship.
cards.fact: HMS Beagle was a small survey ship, only about ninety feet long, sent to chart the coasts of South America. Her voyage was meant to take two years and lasted almost five.
cards.art: HMS Beagle in 1834, lying at anchor in a narrow channel at the far southern tip of South America: a small, sturdy wooden ship with three masts, her sails furled, a white band along her dark hull and boats slung at her sides and stern. She is dwarfed by what stands behind her: a wall of dark beech forest rising straight from the water, and above it a great mountain of blue ice and snow whose glacier comes down to the sea. One of the ship's boats is pulling for the shore with a few men and a pile of boxes and nets. On the cramped deck and hanging in the rigging, small but plain to see, are the collector's things: crates, glass jars, a net, bones laid out to dry. Cold clear light, seabirds, a whale's back in the channel. Seen from the water, the ship in the middle and the mountain in the upper half. Historically accurate: no steam funnel, no gun smoke. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain cloud on the mountain.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. The ship's length (90 feet) and the two years planned are standard, written from memory.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: Gold was lying in a river for whoever came.
cards.fact: Gold was found at a sawmill in California in January 1848. Within two years about a hundred thousand people had come by wagon and by ship, from as far away as Chile, China and Australia.
cards.art: A miner's pan in a California river in 1849, seen close from above: a wide, shallow iron pan held tilted in two wet, cracked hands just under the surface of clear fast water, with a crescent of black sand left along its lower edge, and in the black sand a scatter of bright yellow flakes and one small nugget. The water swirling out of the pan carries away the pale gravel. Around the hands are river stones, a pick, a worn boot planted in the stream. In the upper half of the picture the river runs away up a canyon past a wooden rocker box, two canvas tents, a mule and pine trees, and three other diggers, each different: a Chinese miner in a wide hat, a Chilean in a poncho, a sailor. Hard mountain light. No faces close up. Historically accurate: no machinery, no town. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pines and sky.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: For a day the men on both sides would not fight.
cards.fact: On Christmas Eve of 1914, in the first winter of the First World War, soldiers in the trenches of both sides began singing carols across the lines. In many places they climbed out next day to shake hands, swap small gifts and bury their dead, and here and there kicked a football about.
cards.art: Christmas morning of 1914 between the trenches in Flanders: a flat field white with frost under a pale sun, crossed by two tangles of barbed wire. Out in the middle stand six soldiers, three of each army and each one different, their rifles left behind: men in khaki greatcoats and soft caps, and men in grey with round caps or a spiked helmet with a cloth cover. One of each is shaking hands; two more are trading a tin and a handful of cigars, and one has put on the other's helmet and is being laughed at. Along the parapet of the farther trench stands a row of tiny fir trees with candles. Nobody else is in the picture. Breath smokes in the cold. Seen from the lip of the nearer trench, the meeting in the middle of the picture. No fighting, no bodies, no tanks. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pale winter sky.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. Standard, written from memory.

links.eleanor>magnacarta: King John, who was made to put his seal to Magna Carta in 1215, was Eleanor of Aquitaine's youngest son.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The king's men were stopped by the law.
cards.fact: In 1215 the barons of England forced King John to put his seal to a long list of promises, among them that no free man would be jailed except by the law of the land. Four copies written out that summer still exist.
cards.art: The sealing of Magna Carta in a meadow beside the Thames in June 1215, seen close across a table: a single large sheet of parchment covered edge to edge with small, close writing lies on a cloth, and a clerk's hands are pressing a lump of soft green wax, hung from the foot of the sheet on a cord, between the two halves of a great seal press. Around the table stand the people who matter, cut off at the chest so that we see only hands and belts: on one side several men in mail with their gloved hands resting on their sword hilts, on the other a hand heavy with rings that grips the table's edge, and between them a bishop's hand raised to keep the peace. Grass, a striped tent pole, river light. No faces. Historically accurate: the king does not sign with a pen, no crown on the table, no writing that can be read. The parchment and the seal are in the middle of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain tent cloth.
cards.check: The sealing at Runnymede and the four copies were confirmed. The search did not return the wording of the clause or that John was Eleanor's youngest son; both are standard.

links.aeschylus>marathonmarch: Aeschylus fought in the Athenian line at Marathon, where his brother was killed.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: Having won one battle, they got up and marched to the next.
cards.fact: After beating the Persians on the beach at Marathon in 490 BC, the Athenians saw the enemy fleet put to sea and make for their undefended city. They hurried the twenty-five miles home, and were waiting above the shore when the ships arrived.
cards.art: The Athenian army after the battle of Marathon in 490 BC, hurrying home to save its city, seen from the road ahead: four tired Greek foot soldiers coming toward us along a dusty coast road between pines, each different in age and build, bronze helmets pushed back on their heads, big round shields slung on their backs, long spears on their shoulders, grey with dust and sweat and none of them stopping. The nearest, a man of thirty-five with a bandaged forearm, drinks from a skin as he walks; behind him a grey-bearded man has his arm around a limping boy of eighteen, and a fourth looks out to sea. On the bright water to the right, level with them and going the same way, three dark ships under oar and sail are racing them along the coast. The sun is low. Greece in 490 BC: no lone runner collapsing, no capes, no letters on the shields, no column of repeated figures behind them. The nearest man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and pine branches.
cards.check: Herodotus 6.116. The search corrected the first draft: some scholars put the march on the day after the battle.

links.beethoven>ninth: The Ode to Joy is the last movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, first played in Vienna in 1824.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: The audience would not let the evening end.
cards.fact: At the first performance of his Ninth Symphony in 1824, Beethoven stood beside the conductor beating time, too deaf to hear the orchestra or the cheering. One of the singers turned him around by the sleeve so that he could see the audience on its feet.
cards.art: The end of the first performance of the Ninth Symphony, in a theatre in Vienna on 7 May 1824, seen from the back of the stage: in the middle, with his back to the hall, stands a stocky grey-haired man in a dark green coat, still bent over a score on a stand and still beating time with one hand, though the music has stopped. A young woman, one of the solo singers, in a pale high-waisted gown, has stepped up beside him and taken his sleeve in her fingers, and is gently turning him by the arm to face the house. Past them, over the footlights, the hall is a blur of gold light and of white handkerchiefs waved in the air, so that he can see the applause he cannot hear; no faces can be made out. Two players of the orchestra, each different, have lowered their bows and are watching him. Seen from among the choir, the two figures from the knees up in the middle, the hall blazing in the upper half. No piano, no laurel wreath. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark stage curtain.

links.thoreau>saltmarch: Gandhi printed parts of Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience in his own newspaper in 1907, twenty-three years before he walked to the sea.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: By the time it reached the sea, a walk of 79 people had become a crowd two miles long.
cards.fact: It began with Gandhi and 78 companions and took 24 days. By the time they reached the sea the line of walkers was about two miles long, and within the year some sixty thousand people had gone to jail for making or selling salt.
cards.art: The shore at Dandi in western India early in the morning of 6 April 1930, seen very close and low: a thin brown hand and forearm reaching down to lift a small lump of grey mud crusted white with salt from the wet sand at the edge of the sea. The arm comes from a short white homespun wrap; a tall bamboo staff is planted in the sand beside it, and a pair of worn sandals. Behind, out of focus, stand three companions in white homespun and white caps, each different in age and build, one a woman in a white sari with her hands pressed together, and beyond them flat mud, small waves and a pale sunrise. No face in close view, no soldiers, no flags, no rows of repeated figures. The hand and the salt are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dawn sky.

links.douglass>emancipation: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 and again in 1864 to speak to Lincoln for the Black soldiers the Proclamation had brought into the army.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: It brought nearly two hundred thousand new soldiers to one side.
cards.fact: From 1 January 1863 it declared free the people held as slaves in the states at war with the Union, and opened the army and navy to Black men. Nearly two hundred thousand of them served before the war ended.
cards.art: Watch Night, 31 December 1862, in a small wooden church in the American South, a few minutes before midnight, seen from the middle of the room: an old Black man with white hair stands holding up a large silver pocket watch by its chain in the light of a single torch, and four people are gathered close around him, each different: a boy of ten with his hand raised, counting; a mother lifting a baby to see; a woman praying with her eyes shut; a young man in a soldier's blue coat at the open door. Everyone else in the church is lost in darkness. On the wall hangs a printed notice. All the light comes from the torch, gold on their faces. No chains, no overseer, no writing that can be read, no rows of repeated figures. The old man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark rafters.
cards.check: The search did not return Douglass's night at Tremont Temple, so the link now gives his two visits to Lincoln.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A rider with a foot braced on each side can stay in the saddle all day and go farther.
cards.fact: The oldest pair of stirrups that can be dated lay in the tomb of a nobleman buried in the north of China in 415. With a foot braced on each side a rider could stay in the saddle all day and stand up in it to fight.
cards.art: One early stirrup of north China, about the year 415, seen very close and large from the side as it hangs against the flank of a standing horse: a rounded loop a little wider than a foot, with a flat tread at the bottom and a long straight handle rising from its top, made of bent wood covered in thin gilded bronze held by small rivets, hung by a plain leather strap from a wooden saddle with a high bow in front and behind. A rider's soft felt boot rests in the loop; only the leg below the knee is in the picture. The horse is a short, stocky steppe horse with a thick mane, and the second stirrup shows under its belly on the far side. Dry grass and low hills behind, evening light on the gilding. Historically accurate: no spurs, no horseshoes, no iron plate armour on the horse. The stirrup is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: The pair from the tomb of Feng Sufu (415) was confirmed as the earliest that can be dated; a tomb figure of 322 near Nanjing already shows a pair.

links.astrolabe>sextant: Before the sextant, sailors found how far north or south they were by measuring the height of the Sun with a seagoing astrolabe.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A ship that knows where it is can sail straight for its mark.
cards.fact: A sextant measures how high the Sun or a star stands above the horizon, and from that a navigator can work out how far north or south the ship is. Its curved scale is one sixth of a circle, which gave it its name. The first one was made in London in 1757.
cards.art: A brass sextant of about 1760 held up to the eye on the deck of a sailing ship, seen close from the side: a flat frame shaped like a slice of pie, about as wide as a forearm is long, with a curved scale along its lower edge marked in fine lines, a small telescope along the top, two little mirrors, and a swinging arm with a clamp that the navigator's right thumb is turning. His left hand steadies the frame by its wooden handle. Only the hands, the cuffs of a dark blue coat and part of a cheek and a tricorn hat are in the picture. Beyond the instrument are a ship's rail, a taut rope and the hard line of the sea's horizon with a low Sun on it, which the instrument is aimed at. Historically accurate: no numbers that can be read, no plastic, no later micrometer drum. The sextant is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: John Hadley's octant of 1731 came first; Captain John Campbell had it widened to a sixth of a circle in 1757, and John Bird made that first sextant. The link to the seagoing astrolabe is standard and was not searched.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: Where one river ended the canoe was carried to the next, so a journey did not stop.
cards.fact: The peoples of the northern forests of America built canoes of birch bark, stitched with spruce root and sealed with gum over a light wooden frame. A small one weighs about fifty pounds, no more than a child of seven, so a traveller could paddle to the end of one river and carry the canoe to the next.
cards.art: A birchbark canoe of the Ojibwe, about 1600, being carried over a portage trail between two lakes, seen from the side: one man walks with the canoe upside down on his shoulders, its middle bar across them and his hands holding the edges, so that it covers him to the chest. The canoe is about fourteen feet long, more than twice his height, with both ends curving up to a blunt point; its bark is pale gold with dark horizontal flecks, sewn in panels with neat stitches of root, the seams sealed with black gum. He wears a hide shirt, leggings and moccasins and has a paddle tied inside the canoe. Behind him a woman of the same people follows with a pack on a strap across her forehead. Birch and spruce trees, a rocky path, bright water ahead. Only these two people. Historically accurate: no feather headdress, no painted designs on the bark, no metal fittings. The canoe runs across the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and leaves.
cards.check: Spruce root and spruce gum were confirmed (the United States National Park Service at Grand Portage), and a weight of about fifty pounds for a Wabanaki canoe. The year is only a place on the timeline: these canoes are far older.

links.pachacuti>ropebridge: The Inca roads, with their hanging bridges, grew with the empire that Pachacuti began.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A bridge across a gorge saved days of climbing down one side and up the other.
cards.fact: The Inca crossed the gorges of the Andes on hanging bridges made of twisted grass. One of them still hangs over the Apurímac River in Peru, about thirty yards from cliff to cliff: every June the people of four villages cut the old bridge down and weave a new one in three days.
cards.art: A hanging bridge of twisted grass rope across a deep, narrow river gorge in the high Andes, seen from one end looking along it: four cables as thick as a man's thigh form the floor, laid with a mat of sticks, and two thinner cables at waist height form the handrails, laced to the floor with a web of cord on each side, so that the whole bridge sags in a long curve from stone footings on this cliff to stone footings on the far one. The rope is the colour of straw, fresh and bright. One woman in a full dark skirt, a woven shawl and a flat hat is halfway across, small against the gorge, holding both rails; nobody else is on it. Far below, green river water; above, bare brown slopes. Historically accurate: no steel wire, no planks, no metal posts. The bridge runs from the lower left up to the right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and rock.
cards.check: The yearly rebuilding in June by four Quechua communities, over three days, was confirmed; its length is given as 28 or 30 metres. That the road system grew under Pachacuti and his heirs is standard and was not returned.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A load that rolls goes much farther in a day than a load that is carried.
cards.fact: The oldest wooden wheel yet found was dug out of a marsh in Slovenia in 2002 with its axle beside it. It is about 5,200 years old and is made of two planks of ash. Its square hole shows that wheel and axle were wedged together and turned as one.
cards.art: The oldest wooden wheel known, as it was about 3150 BC, on a two-wheeled cart standing at the edge of a lake village in central Europe, seen close from the side and a little below: a solid disc of pale ash wood about two and a half feet across, made of two planks joined edge to edge by four dark wooden battens let into grooves, with a square hole at the centre in which a square-ended oak axle is wedged tight. The cart is a simple wooden frame with a pole in front; one ox, in true proportion, stands yoked to it with its head turned away. Mud and reeds underfoot, the stilts of a house on posts over the water behind. No people. Historically accurate: no spokes, no metal rim, no nails. The wheel fills the middle and right of the picture in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: Found in 2002; the age is given as 5,100 to 5,350 years. Ash wheel, oak axle, square hole and wedges were confirmed.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Every count in the empire could be read off the cords.
cards.fact: The Inca kept the counts of a whole empire, its people, its llamas and its stores of maize, on knotted cords instead of in writing. The kind of knot and its place on the cord gave the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Herders in the Andes still keep count of their animals this way.
cards.art: An Inca quipu of about 1450 held up and spread out by two hands, seen close from the front: one thick main cord held level between the hands, and from it some forty thin cords of cotton hanging straight down like a fringe, dyed in plain colours, cream, brown, dark blue, red and green, each with clusters of small knots tied at three or four different heights so that the knots line up in rows across the fringe. A few of the hanging cords have a shorter cord tied to them. Only the hands and the edge of a tunic woven with small squares are in the picture. Behind, out of focus, a wall of close-fitted grey stone and a row of storehouses on a hillside. Historically accurate: no beads, no feathers, no writing. The cords hang right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain stone wall and sky.
cards.check: The place-value knots and the herders who still use them were confirmed. Several hundred quipus survive; nobody has an exact count.

links.@silk>starchart: The chart was found in 1907 in a sealed cave at Dunhuang, an oasis town on the Silk Road.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: A map of the whole sky, to be read a little further every night.
cards.fact: This paper scroll from Tang dynasty China is the oldest complete map of the night sky known from anywhere. It shows more than 1,300 stars in ink, group by group, and it lay with some forty thousand other manuscripts in a sealed cave until 1907.
cards.art: A Chinese star chart of about the year 670, a long narrow scroll of fine yellowed paper, partly unrolled on a low wooden table and seen from above at a slant: across it run groups of stars drawn as small circles in black, red and white-with-a-black-rim, joined into figures by thin straight ink lines, with a short column of brush writing beside each group, and at the unrolled end a round map of the stars about the pole. One hand in a wide grey sleeve holds the roll open while the other points with a thin bamboo stick at a group shaped like a ladle. An oil lamp, an ink stone and a brush stand at the edge; through a doorway behind are desert cliffs under a real night sky. No face. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no constellation pictures of animals or people, no telescope. The scroll fills the middle of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wall and night sky.
cards.check: A study of 2009 counts 1,339 stars and dates it 649 to 684; an older estimate was about 940.

links.galileo>telescope: Galileo heard in 1609 of a Dutch spyglass, built better ones himself, and turned them on the sky.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Every clear night it showed something nobody had seen before.
cards.fact: Galileo's telescope was a tube with a glass lens at each end that made things look twenty times closer. In January 1610 he watched four small lights beside Jupiter change places from night to night, and understood that they were moons circling another world.
cards.art: Galileo's telescope of 1609 on a wooden stand at an open window in Padua, at night, seen close from the side: a slender tube about as long as a walking stick and no thicker than a wrist, made of wood covered in dark red leather with bands of gold tooling, a little wider where the lens sits at the far end, resting in a simple forked stand and pointed up at the sky. On the windowsill beside it lies an open notebook with a row of small ink drawings, each a circle with three or four dots beside it in different places. Outside, over tiled roofs and one dome, a single bright planet stands in a clear dark sky with four tiny points of light in a line beside it. No people. Historically accurate: no tripod of metal, no eyepiece at the side, no mirror. The tube runs from the lower left to the upper right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain night sky and window frame.
cards.check: Britannica: he heard of the Dutch instrument in spring 1609, was observing at twenty times by the autumn and found the four moons in January 1610. Other accounts give his best telescope thirty times.

links.@timbuktu>manuscripts: The books were written and copied in Timbuktu, and families there have kept them from parent to child ever since.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: A city's learning, kept and copied in its own houses.
cards.fact: Families in Timbuktu have handed down handwritten books for hundreds of years, most of them in Arabic. When armed men seized the city in 2012, its librarians packed some 350,000 of them into ordinary metal trunks and sent them south to safety by road and by canoe on the Niger.
cards.art: A manuscript of Timbuktu lying open in a tin trunk, seen close from above at a slant: a book of loose leaves of thick cream paper, not sewn, kept in a worn wrapper of red-brown tooled leather with a flap, its two open pages covered with neat lines of brown and black handwriting that runs from right to left, with notes written slantwise in the margins and one diagram of circles in red. The trunk is an ordinary painted metal one, half full of other books in their leather wrappers, stacked flat. A pair of hands in the sleeves of a pale blue robe is lowering one more book in. Mud-brick wall, a strip of hard sunlight across the floor, a little sand. No face. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no printed pages, no gold. The open book is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain mud wall.
cards.check: The trunks, the roads and the canoes on the Niger were confirmed. Counts of what was moved run from about 278,000 to 400,000. What the books are about was not returned, so the fact does not list it.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: News that took days by horse arrived in a moment.
cards.fact: On 24 May 1844 Samuel Morse tapped out a message in dots and dashes at the Capitol in Washington, and it was read in Baltimore at the same moment. By 1861 a wire ran across the United States, and five years later another lay under the Atlantic.
cards.art: A telegraph key and register of 1844 on a plain table, seen close from the side: a small brass lever on a wooden base, with a round black knob that one finger is pressing down, wired to a brass machine beside it in which a clockwork roller is drawing a narrow paper tape past a pointed arm; the tape curls out across the table marked with a row of short and long dents. Two cloth-covered wires run from the machine up the wall and out through a window frame to a wooden pole with glass knobs. Only the hand, a white cuff and a dark coat sleeve are in the picture. An oil lamp, a glass jar battery with metal plates. Historically accurate: no telephone, no light bulb, no letters or numbers that can be read. The key and the tape are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall.
cards.check: 24 May 1844, the line across the United States (October 1861) and the lasting Atlantic cable (July 1866) were confirmed.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Books opened to readers who could not see them.
cards.fact: Louis Braille lost his sight as a small boy. At school in Paris he was shown a soldier's code of raised dots for reading in the dark, and by the age of fifteen he had cut it down to a cell of six dots that one fingertip can cover. Those six dots make 63 different signs.
cards.art: A page of braille being read by touch about 1830, seen very close from the side and a little above: a sheet of thick cream paper on a sloping wooden desk, covered with rows of small raised dots that catch the light from a window so that each dot throws a tiny shadow, and across one row the first two fingers of a boy's hand moving from left to right, the fingertips resting lightly on the dots. Beside the page lie the tools that made it: a flat brass frame with rows of small windows, hinged over another sheet, and a short awl with a round wooden handle. Only the hands and the cuffs of a dark school uniform are in the picture. Historically accurate: no printed letters, no pen and ink on the page, no spectacles. The page and the fingers are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window light.
cards.check: The soldier's code (Charles Barbier's night writing), the six dots at fifteen in 1824 and the 63 signs were confirmed. Most sources say he was hurt at three; one says four.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Once a thing was pressed into clay it no longer had to be remembered.
cards.fact: The oldest writing we know is on small tablets of clay from the city of Uruk, in what is now Iraq. They are not stories or prayers but accounts: so much grain, so many sheep, so much beer for the workers. About six thousand of these earliest tablets have been found.
cards.art: One of the earliest written tablets, from Uruk about 3200 BC, held in the palm of a hand and seen very close: a small cushion of pale brown clay no bigger than a playing card, its face divided into boxes by scratched lines, and in each box a few simple signs pressed in while the clay was wet, a jar with a pointed base, an ear of barley, a head beside a bowl, with rows of round and wedge-shaped dents beside them for numbers. The other hand holds a cut reed with its tip resting in the last box. Only the hands and bare forearms are in the picture. Behind, out of focus, big clay jars standing in rows against a mud-brick wall. Historically accurate: pictures and number dents, not the later wedge writing; nothing that reads as a modern letter or numeral. The tablet is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain mud-brick wall.
cards.check: Sources date the first tablets between 3300 and 3000 BC. The six thousand tablets and the beer rations (a tablet in the British Museum) were confirmed.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: It carried whole families to islands thousands of miles away.
cards.fact: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific in canoes with two hulls, steering by the stars, the swells and the flight of birds. A canoe some sixty feet long could carry two dozen people with their pigs, dogs, chickens and young plants, enough to settle an island.
cards.art: A Polynesian voyaging canoe far out on the open Pacific about a thousand years ago, just after sunset, seen from the water astern and to one side: two long slender hulls joined side by side by a platform of lashed poles, with a small thatched shelter on it, driven by two tall sails shaped like a crab's claw, woven of pale matting. The canoe rides up the face of a long ocean swell. In the stern the navigator stands braced at a great steering paddle, an older man in a wrapped bark-cloth garment, his face lifted to the first bright star low ahead. Three other people are aboard, each different: a woman tending young plants wrapped in leaves, a boy bailing, a man asleep against a basket; a pig and gourds of water beside them. Two white sea birds fly the same way overhead. Historically accurate: two hulls, not one hull with a float; no carved figurehead, no flower garlands, no compass. The sails are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain darkening sky.
cards.check: Sizes differ: canoes of fifty to sixty feet for two dozen people (PBS), about twenty metres as a rule (Te Ara). When each island group was settled is still argued over, so the fact gives no dates.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: It could cross a sea and then be rowed far up a river.
cards.fact: A longship was long, light and so shallow that it could be rowed up a river or run straight onto a beach. One built in Norway about 890, with places for 32 oars, was dug out of a burial mound almost whole in 1880, and in 1893 a copy of it crossed the Atlantic in about four weeks.
cards.art: A Viking ship of about 890, the one found at Gokstad, under sail on a grey northern sea, seen from the water off her bow and a little below: a long, low, open ship of overlapping oak planks, about fourteen times as long as a man is tall, sharp and high at both ends with plain curved stems, a single mast with one great square sail of wool in broad stripes, and a row of round shields, alternately black and yellow, hung along the rail. A big steering oar is fixed to the right side near the stern, held by the one man standing there; four other men, each different, sit on sea chests or haul on a rope. Spray, gulls, a line of mountains far off. Historically accurate: no horned helmets, no dragon head on this ship, no cabin or deck house. The sail is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain cloudy sky.
cards.check: Built about 890, 32 oars, about 24 metres long and dug up in 1880: confirmed. The copy named Viking crossed in 1893 in 22 or 27 days, depending on the source.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: He took a whole ship's company out from under the guns to the other side.
cards.fact: Before dawn on 13 May 1862 Robert Smalls, the enslaved pilot of a Confederate steamer in Charleston, put on the captain's straw hat, picked up his own family and the families of his crew, and steamed out past the harbour forts, giving the right signal at each. He handed the ship to the Union fleet.
cards.art: The steamer Planter leaving Charleston harbour at about half past four in the morning of 13 May 1862, seen from the water off her bow: a low wooden side-wheel steamer with one tall black funnel, a big paddle box on each side and a small wheelhouse on top, moving quietly through grey water in the half-dark before dawn. At the open window of the wheelhouse stands one man, a young Black man of twenty-three in a captain's white jacket and a wide straw hat pulled low, his arms folded on the sill the way the captain stood, one hand reaching for the whistle cord. No one else is on deck. Behind and above the ship rises the dark brick wall of a fort on its island, with one lantern and one small sentry on the parapet. Historically accurate: no flag flying yet, no smoke of gunfire, no people in chains. The wheelhouse and the man are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The captain's hat, the signals at Fort Sumter at about 4.15 to 4.30 in the morning and the families taken aboard were confirmed. How many people were on the ship was not returned, so the fact gives no number.

links.champollion>hieroglyphs: On 27 September 1822 Champollion's letter was read out in Paris, showing how the hieroglyphs spell names by their sounds.
links.rosetta>hieroglyphs: The Greek on the Rosetta Stone told scholars what the Egyptian beside it had to say.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: A dead script could suddenly be read, and with it everything written in it.
cards.fact: In the ancient writing of Egypt the names of kings and queens are ringed with an oval. Champollion matched the signs inside two of those ovals, Ptolemy and Cleopatra, with the same names in Greek, and so had the sounds of a dozen signs. With them he went on to read names that no Greek had written down.
cards.art: A scholar's desk in Paris in September 1822, seen close from above at a slant: a large sheet of paper on which two long ovals have been copied in ink, each holding a short row of small Egyptian picture signs, a lion, a mouth, a reed, a square, a bird, and under each sign a pencilled Greek letter, with lines drawn from the signs the two ovals share. One hand holds a pencil on the last sign; the other pins down a printed drawing of a carved stone. Around the sheet lie a candle burned low, a stack of worn grammars, a cup, and a small plaster cast of a carved oval. Only the hands and frayed cuffs are in the picture. Grey morning light from a window. Historically accurate: the signs are true hieroglyphs in two ovals, no pyramids, no mummy, no writing in modern letters that can be read. The sheet is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: The letter (read on 27 September, signed on the 22nd) and the twelve signs won from the ovals of Ptolemy and Cleopatra were confirmed; so was his reading of the name Ramesses from Abu Simbel on 14 September.

links.newton>halley: Edmond Halley used Newton's law of gravity to show that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one comet coming back.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: It came back, as he had said it would.
cards.fact: Edmond Halley worked out that one comet had been seen three times, about 76 years apart, and said it would be back around 1758. He died in 1742. On Christmas night of 1758 a farmer near Dresden who watched the sky as a hobby found it with his own telescope, the first return of a comet ever foretold.
cards.art: Christmas night of 1758 on a farm near Dresden, seen from the yard: a broad-shouldered farmer of about thirty-five in a heavy coat, knitted cap and wooden clogs stands in the snow with his eye to a long brass telescope that rests on the top bar of a gate, pointed low over the roof of a timbered barn. In the clear black sky over the barn, among sharp winter stars, hangs a small soft patch of light with a short faint tail. A lantern stands in the snow at his feet beside an open notebook, and his breath smokes. Nobody else; one warm window in the farmhouse behind. Historically accurate: the comet is small and dim, not a blazing streak; no observatory dome, no wig. The comet is in the upper half, right of centre; the man stands lower left. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain black sky with a few stars.
cards.check: Johann Georg Palitzsch, farmer and amateur astronomer, 25 December 1758 (one source says Christmas Eve), and Halley's death in 1742 were confirmed.

links.magellan>naovictoria: The Victoria was the last of the five ships that Magellan led out of Spain in 1519.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: Her one cargo of cloves paid for the whole voyage.
cards.fact: On 6 September 1522 one small, leaking ship, the Victoria, reached Spain from the south with eighteen men on board, three years after sailing west. She was the first ship to go around the world. The cloves in her hold were worth more than the whole fleet of five ships had cost.
cards.art: The ship Victoria coming into the mouth of a Spanish river in September 1522, seen from a small boat alongside: a short, round-bellied wooden ship with three masts, her paint gone, her sails patched and grey, weed along her waterline, and a thin stream of water running from a pump over her side. At the rail stand three of her crew, each different and all of them thin and bearded in rags, one shading his eyes toward the shore, one holding a pump handle, one with a candle. In the foreground, in the small boat, an open sack spills dark brown cloves, each like a small nail with a round head, across a plank. Low sandy shore, a white church tower, hard afternoon light. Historically accurate: no gun smoke, no crowd on the quay, no later galleon's high carved stern. The ship's hull and masts are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: 6 September 1522 at Sanlúcar and the eighteen men were confirmed (some lists count seventeen Europeans and the men taken on in Asia). Sources say the cloves, about 26 tons, covered the cost of the expedition or were worth twice as much.

links.archimedes>syracuse: Archimedes designed the machines on the walls of Syracuse, his own city, when the Romans attacked it from the sea.

cards.tx: Quick. One of your Figures gets +2 Might for one clash. On the other player's turn it plays itself when it would save your Figure, paid for with 1 Spark you kept.
cards.fit: His machines saved the wall at the moment the attack came.
cards.fact: When a Roman fleet came against Syracuse in 213 BC, the historian Polybius says, beams swung out over the walls and dropped great weights on the ships, and iron claws caught others by the bow and stood them on end. The city held out for more than a year.
