cards.art: The sea wall of Syracuse in 213 BC, seen from the water below and to one side: a high wall of pale stone blocks rising straight from the sea, and over its top a great wooden beam, as long as the wall is tall, swung out on a pivot like the arm of a crane. From the beam's end a chain runs down to an iron grapple with three hooks that has caught the bow of one Roman warship and is hauling it up out of the water, so that the ship stands tilted on its stern with its oars hanging loose and water pouring off it. Three soldiers, each different, cling to its rail. On the wall, small, two men haul on the beam's other end with ropes. A second ship is backing away at the lower left. Historically accurate: one ship lifted, no mirrors, no fire, no rows of identical soldiers. The beam and the lifted bow are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: Polybius (Histories 8.6) was confirmed for the weights and the claws; the siege ran from spring 213 to the autumn of 212. Whether a claw could lift a large warship is still argued about, so the fact gives it as his account.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: A spoiled dish turned out to be a find.
cards.fact: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to his laboratory in London and found that mould had got into one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould the bacteria had gone. The medicine made from that mould, penicillin, was ready for patients in the 1940s.
cards.art: A round glass dish held up to a window in a London hospital laboratory in September 1928, seen very close: a shallow dish about as wide as a hand, its floor covered with a thin layer of clear jelly dotted all over with small cream-coloured spots, and near one edge a single large fluffy patch of pale blue-green mould with a white rim. All around that patch there is a clear ring where the spots have vanished. Two fingers and a thumb hold the dish by its edge; a white coat cuff shows. Behind, out of focus, a crowded bench of other dishes in stacks, a brass microscope, a rack of glass tubes, a window with brick chimneys beyond. No face. Historically accurate: glass, not plastic; no rubber gloves, no printed labels that can be read. The dish is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: 3 September 1928 and the dish were confirmed. Where he had been on holiday differs between sources, and one writer doubts the usual story because his first notebook entry is dated 30 October.

links.shakespeare>folio: Seven years after Shakespeare died, two actors of his own company gathered his plays into one book.
links.press>folio: About 750 copies were printed in London, and some 230 of them still exist.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: About half his plays came down to us through this one book.
cards.fact: In 1623 John Heminges and Henry Condell, who had acted beside Shakespeare, had 36 of his plays printed in one large book. About half of them had never been printed before, among them Macbeth, Julius Caesar, Twelfth Night and The Tempest, and without the book they would probably be lost.
cards.art: A printer's workshop in London in 1623, seen close across a table: a tall stack of large printed sheets, folded once and gathered but not yet bound, the top sheet showing a page of two columns of small print inside ruled borders, and beside the stack one finished copy bound in plain brown calfskin, as tall as a forearm, lying shut. Two men stand over them, seen from the chest down so that we see hands and aprons more than faces: one older, in an actor's good black doublet, laying a bundle of worn handwritten playbooks tied with string on the table; the other a printer in an inky apron, lifting a fresh sheet by its corners. Behind them the wooden frame and screw of a press and sheets hung over cords to dry. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no portrait showing, no quill being used. The stack and the book are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark beams.
cards.check: Heminges and Condell, the 36 plays, about 750 copies and 230 to 235 survivors were confirmed. That eighteen of the plays were first printed here is standard and was not returned, so the fact says about half.

links.michelangelo>david: Michelangelo was twenty-nine when his David was unveiled in Florence.

cards.fit: A giant came to stand at the city's door.
cards.fact: Michelangelo's David is seventeen feet tall, about three times the height of a man. It took forty men four days to move it the half mile from his workshop to the main square of Florence, hanging upright in a wooden cage that rolled on greased beams. It was unveiled there on 8 September 1504.
cards.art: The moving of Michelangelo's David through a street of Florence in 1504, seen from the street ahead and a little below: the white marble statue of a standing naked youth, about three times the height of the men around it, hangs upright from thick ropes inside a tall open cage of heavy timbers, swaying a little clear of its floor, its weight on the right leg, the left hand raised to the shoulder, the head turned to its left. The cage stands on greased wooden beams laid on the paving. Four workmen, each different in age and dress, are at work: two lean on a lever at the back, one carries a beam forward, one pours grease from a pot. A boy watches from a doorway. Narrow street of plain stone houses, morning light on the marble. Historically accurate: the statue is finished and unbroken, no fig leaf, no pedestal yet, no rows of identical workers. The statue's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky between the roofs.
cards.check: The height (5.17 metres), the forty men, four days, the cage on greased beams and 8 September 1504 were confirmed. Sources give the arrival in the square as 18 May or 8 June.

cards.fit: The uproar in the hall stopped everything else.
cards.fact: At the first night of Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring, in Paris on 29 May 1913, people in the audience shouted, whistled and argued so loudly that the dancers could not hear the orchestra. Most accounts say the man who had made the dance, Nijinsky, called the counts to them from the side of the stage.
cards.art: The side of the stage at a Paris theatre on 29 May 1913, seen from the wings: in the near shadow a slight young man in evening dress stands on a wooden chair, one hand gripping a rope, the other beating the air, his mouth open, calling numbers toward the stage. Out in the light three dancers, each different, are caught in the middle of a heavy, flat-footed jump with their knees bent and feet turned in, wearing long belted smocks painted with bands of red and blue patterns, soft boots bound with cross-straps, and long braids or pointed caps. Beyond them, across the footlights, the dark hall shows only as a few white shirt fronts and raised programmes. Historically accurate: no tutus, no pointe shoes, no rows of identical dancers. The man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark curtain.
cards.check: The date, the theatre and the noise were confirmed. Stravinsky said Nijinsky shouted the counts from a chair in the wings; the company's stage manager remembered him standing silent, so the fact says most accounts.

cards.fit: Shut out of the hall, she sang all the same.
cards.fact: In 1939 the great singer Marian Anderson was refused the biggest concert hall in Washington because she was Black. So on Easter Sunday she sang from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead, in the open air, to 75,000 people and to millions more by radio.
cards.art: Marian Anderson singing on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on 9 April 1939, seen from the side and a little below: a tall, composed Black woman of forty-two in a long dark fur coat with a bright scarf at the throat and a small dark hat, standing very straight with her eyes closed and her hands clasped in front of her, before a cluster of six old-fashioned radio microphones on thin stands. Behind her rise two of the great fluted white columns of the memorial, and between them, in shadow, the seated marble figure can just be made out. A grand piano and its player, a man in a dark overcoat, are at the left edge. The listeners are not shown except as a soft band of colour far below. Cold bright afternoon. Historically accurate: no stage, no banner, no modern loudspeakers, no rows of faces. Her head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pale sky and stone.
cards.check: Easter Sunday 9 April 1939, the 75,000 and the refusal of Constitution Hall by the Daughters of the American Revolution were confirmed; the society itself said the hall was already booked that day. Her coat and the microphones in the picture brief are from the photographs and need a check against them.

cards.fit: A franc a seat, and before long the seats were full all day.
cards.fact: On 28 December 1895, in a basement room of a café in Paris, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten films, each less than a minute long, to people who had paid one franc. Fewer than forty came that first evening.
cards.art: The first paid film show, in a basement room in Paris on 28 December 1895, seen from behind the projector: in the foreground a wooden box no bigger than a hat box stands on a tall stand, with a brass lens in front and a small crank handle that one hand is turning, a lamp house behind it throwing a cone of light through the dark room. On a white cloth screen at the far end is a grey moving picture of a factory gate with people walking out of it, among them a woman in a wide hat and a man pushing a bicycle. Between the projector and the screen sit only five spectators on cane chairs, seen from behind, each different: a man in a top hat leaning forward, a woman with her hand to her mouth, a boy standing up. Historically accurate: the picture on the screen is black and white and silent, no train rushing at the audience, no rows of identical heads. The screen is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wall.
cards.check: The date, the Salon Indien of the Grand Café, the ten films and the one franc were confirmed; the audience is given as 33, 35 or about 40. A paid show in Berlin by the Skladanowsky brothers was eight weeks earlier, so the card does not call this the first.

cards.tx: Swap two Figures at different Places. At least one must be yours.
cards.fit: Two men changed places across a line.
cards.fact: On the morning of 10 February 1962 two prisoners walked past each other on a bridge at the edge of Berlin, between East and West: Francis Gary Powers, an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union, and Rudolf Abel, a Soviet spy caught in New York. Each went home.
cards.art: The Glienicke Bridge on the cold morning of 10 February 1962, seen from one bank looking along it: a long steel bridge of green-painted girders in low arches, its roadway empty and wet, with a white line painted across the middle. On the line two men are passing each other, walking in opposite directions, each alone: one tall and young in a heavy coat and a Russian fur hat, carrying a small case; the other thin, older and bald, in a dark overcoat, hatless, carrying a bundle. They do not look at each other. At each end of the bridge, small and far apart, stand two men in overcoats and one parked car. Bare trees, mist on the river. Historically accurate: morning, not night; no searchlights, no soldiers in rows, no barbed wire on the bridge. The two men are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain grey sky.
cards.check: The date, the bridge, the two men and the morning hour were confirmed. A third man, the American student Frederic Pryor, was freed at Checkpoint Charlie as part of the same bargain.

links.caesar>rubicon: In January of 49 BC Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon, the small river that marked the edge of Italy.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: He was over the line and far down the road before anyone could stop him.
cards.fact: A Roman general had to give up his army before he came home to Italy. In January of 49 BC Julius Caesar crossed the little river Rubicon, the border, with a single legion at his back. From that step there was no going back, and it began a civil war.
cards.art: The river Rubicon on a January night in 49 BC, seen from the far bank looking back across the ford: a stream so narrow and shallow that a horse could cross it in six strides, running between low banks of frosted reeds. In mid-stream a lean, balding Roman of fifty on a bay horse, bareheaded, in a red cloak over a plain leather cuirass, has reined in and is looking down at the water under his horse's knees. Behind him on the bank, lit by two torches, three soldiers of the late Republic, each different, wait to follow, in mail shirts with oval shields and plain bronze helmets, one holding a standard topped with a silver eagle. Mist, a leafless willow, stars. Historically accurate: the horse is larger than the man and in true proportion, no laurel wreath, no rectangular shields, no rows of identical soldiers. The rider's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain night sky.
cards.check: The Thirteenth Legion, January of 49 BC and the law were confirmed. The day is usually given as 10 January, but neither the date nor the exact stream is certain.

links.menelik>adwa: Menelik II led the armies of Ethiopia at Adwa on 1 March 1896.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: The whole country came to stand in one place.
cards.fact: Lords from every part of Ethiopia brought their soldiers to Adwa to stand with the emperor Menelik and the empress Taytu. On the night before 1 March 1896 three Italian columns set out in the dark along separate mountain tracks to surprise them. The Ethiopians were waiting, and by the end of the day the invaders were beaten.
cards.art: The hills east of Adwa at first light on 1 March 1896, seen from an Ethiopian position looking down a rocky slope: in the foreground three Ethiopian soldiers, each different, wait behind boulders, a grey-bearded nobleman in a lion's-mane headdress and an embroidered cape with a curved sword and a round hide shield studded with silver, a young rifleman in a white cotton wrap with a cartridge belt aiming a breech-loading rifle, and a woman bringing a water gourd. On the next ridge a red, gold and green royal umbrella marks where the emperor and empress stand, small and far off. Down in the valley, small, a short broken line of soldiers in pale uniforms and tropical helmets is coming out of the mist. Steep flat-topped mountains behind. Historically accurate: rifles as well as spears and shields, no close view of wounds, no rows of identical soldiers. The nobleman's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dawn sky.
cards.check: The night march of three brigades by separate tracks, the Ethiopians already in position, Taytu's part beside Menelik and the defeat by the end of the day were confirmed. The dress in the picture brief is from memory and needs a check against photographs and paintings of the time.

cards.fit: They reached the one place nobody had, and had nothing left for more that day.
cards.fact: At half past eleven on the morning of 29 May 1953 the Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay and the New Zealander Edmund Hillary became the first people known to stand on the highest point on Earth. They stayed about fifteen minutes, because their oxygen was running low.
cards.art: The top of Mount Everest at half past eleven on 29 May 1953, seen from a few steps below the summit: a small rounded dome of snow against a sky so dark blue it is almost black, and on it one man standing, Tenzing Norgay, in a bulky blue windproof suit, high boots with metal spikes, thick gloves, a hood and an oxygen mask with goggles pushed up, holding his ice axe above his head with a string of four small flags blowing out from its shaft. A rope runs from his waist down to the lower left corner, where the gloved hand and the box camera of his partner come into the picture. Below and behind them the white ridges of other great mountains fall away under a floor of cloud. Only these two people, and only one of them seen whole. Historically accurate: 1953 clothing and a heavy oxygen frame on his back, no fixed ropes, no ladders, no other climbers. His head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark blue sky.
cards.check: The time, the fifteen minutes, the oxygen and the photograph of Tenzing with the flags of Britain, Nepal, the United Nations and India on his axe were confirmed.

links.ramesses>kadesh: Ramesses II made this peace with the Hittite king Hattusili III in the twenty-first year of his reign.

cards.fit: Two armies that had fought for years put their weapons down.
cards.fact: About 1259 BC the kings of Egypt and of the Hittites swore to end their long war and never to attack each other again. It is the oldest peace treaty whose words survive, and we have both sides' copies: one carved on temple walls in Egypt, the other on clay tablets dug up in Turkey.
cards.art: The treaty between Egypt and the Hittites as it was sent about 1259 BC, seen close on a table of dark wood: a flat tablet of bright silver about the size of a large book, covered with fine rows of small wedge-shaped signs, with a round seal pressed in the middle showing a tiny figure embraced by a taller one. Two hands hold it from opposite sides of the table: one a brown Egyptian hand with a gold bracelet and a pleated white linen sleeve, the other a paler hand in the long woollen sleeve of a Hittite envoy, wearing a seal ring. Between them on the table lie a clay tablet with the same wedge signs and a roll of papyrus. No faces. Sunlight through a doorway, a painted column behind. Historically accurate: wedge signs on the silver, no hieroglyphs on it, no weapons on the table, no writing that can be read. The tablet is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall.
cards.check: The date (1259 or 1258 BC), both versions and the United Nations' own words, the earliest peace treaty whose text is known to have survived, were confirmed. That the treaty was first sent on a silver tablet (picture brief only) is from memory.

links.kublai>typhoon: Kublai Khan sent the fleet against Japan in 1281, seven years after his first one had turned back.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The storm stopped a whole fleet where it lay.
cards.fact: In the summer of 1281 a great fleet sent by Kublai Khan lay off the coast of Japan for weeks, kept from landing by a stone wall twelve miles long around Hakata Bay and by raids in small boats at night. In the middle of August a typhoon struck, and most of the ships were wrecked at their moorings.
cards.art: The typhoon of August 1281 off the coast of Kyushu, seen from the top of the stone sea wall: in the foreground the wall itself, about as high as a man and a half, built of rough fitted stones, and on it two samurai, each different, crouched against the wind, one older in dark laced armour holding his helmet on, one young with a long bow, both looking out to sea. Out in the bay, under a black sky and flying spray, three big wooden ships with high sterns and ribbed matting sails have been driven together; one is rolling over, its mast gone, and broken planks and a great wooden anchor wash in the surf below the wall. Rain in sheets, one break of livid light on the horizon. Historically accurate: only three ships and two men, no lightning dragon, no rows of identical ships or soldiers. The ships are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain storm cloud.
cards.check: The wall of about twelve miles, the mid-August storm and the loss of most of the fleet were confirmed. The fleet was moored off Takashima, west of Hakata Bay, when the storm came. Historians differ on how much the storm, and how much the defenders, decided it.

links.tutankhamun>tomb: The tomb was Tutankhamun's own, sealed some 3,250 years before and still full.

cards.fit: A king's treasure came up into the light.
cards.fact: On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen uncovered a stone step in the floor of the Valley of the Kings; by one account a boy carrying water found it. The steps led down to a sealed door. The last of what lay behind it was not carried out until 1932.
cards.art: The first look into Tutankhamun's tomb on 26 November 1922, seen from inside the dark room looking back at the door: a wall of rough plaster blocks with a small ragged hole broken through its upper corner, and through the hole a hand holding a lit candle and, behind it, one eye and the brim of a hat. The candle's light falls into the room on three things only: the gilded head of a couch carved as a cow with tall horns, the side of a painted wooden chest, and a pile of white egg-shaped boxes. Everything else is black. Dust hangs in the beam. Historically accurate: no electric torch, no golden mask in view, no mummy, no writing that can be read. The hole and the candle are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain darkness.
cards.check: 4 November, the first look on 26 November and the last objects sent to Cairo in 1932 were confirmed; the water boy is given by some accounts only.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: Behind a hole in the ground was a whole lost gallery.
cards.fact: In September 1940 Marcel Ravidat, who was eighteen, and three friends widened a hole left by a fallen tree near the village of Montignac in France and climbed down with a lamp. On the walls were horses, bulls and deer larger than life, painted by people who lived some 17,000 to 20,000 years before.
cards.art: The painted cave of Lascaux on 12 September 1940, seen from the floor looking up: a boy of eighteen in a patched jacket, shorts and heavy boots stands at the lower left with his back half to us, holding up a home-made oil lamp, and its yellow light spreads over a curving wall and ceiling of pale rock covered with animals painted in black, red and ochre: one great bull drawn in black outline, three times as long as the boy is tall, facing a line of small galloping horses with bristly manes, and a red cow leaping above them. A second boy, younger and smaller, is only a pair of legs sliding in through a hole low at the left edge. Nobody else. Historically accurate: the animals are in the true style of the cave, no painted people, no handprints, no electric torch. The bull's head is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark rock.
cards.check: 12 September 1940, Ravidat and his three friends (Jacques Marsal, Georges Agnel, Simon Coencas) were confirmed. Accounts differ on the dog and on whether he first found the hole four days earlier, so the fact leaves both out. The age is given as about 17,000 or nearly 20,000 years.

heldForGuides.tx: Scholar. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
heldForGuides.fact: She found two new elements, polonium and radium, boiling down tons of ore in a leaky shed to win a speck of radium. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
heldForGuides.art: Marie Curie about 1900 in the old shed in Paris where she refined radium, late in the evening: a slight woman of thirty-three with a high forehead, grey eyes and fair hair pinned up loosely, in a plain dark dress under a stained work smock. She has paused in the doorway on her way out and looks back over her shoulder into the dark room, one hand on the frame, her tired face lit faintly blue-green. On rough shelves and a deal table stand rows of small glass tubes and dishes, each glowing softly with the same pale light. In the shadows are an iron stove, a big cast-iron basin and the heavy iron rod, nearly as tall as she is, with which she stirred the boiling ore. heldForGuides.art: Abraham Lincoln in the summer of 1862, in the telegraph office of the War Department, where he went to read the news from the armies and where he began to write the order of emancipation: a very tall, gaunt man of fifty-three with a deeply lined face, a dark beard without a moustache and untidy black hair, in a black frock coat with a grey wool shawl around his shoulders. He sits hunched at a borrowed desk by the window, his long legs folded under it, writing a line slowly on a sheet of foolscap and then gazing out at the street; his tall hat stands upside down on the desk with papers in it. Behind him two young operators bend over clicking brass telegraph keys. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. heldForGuides.tx: Legacy of Gandhi. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
heldForGuides.fact: He spent twenty-seven years in prison for fighting laws that set South Africans apart by the colour of their skin. Four years after he walked free he was elected president, and he asked the country to forgive and not to take revenge.
heldForGuides.art: Nelson Mandela about 1965, aged forty-seven, a prisoner in the lime quarry on Robben Island: a tall, broad-shouldered man with close-cropped hair, a strong jaw and a steady look, in the prison dress given to Black prisoners there, a khaki shirt, short trousers and sandals without socks. He stands in the white glare of the quarry floor with a pick resting head-down on the ground under his folded hands, and has turned to speak to a half circle of other prisoners who sit on blocks of lime in the mouth of a shallow cave cut in the quarry face, one of them drawing in the dust with a finger as if at a lesson. A warder with a rifle stands far off on the rim. Everything is bleached white and the men squint against it. Seen from the cave mouth, Mandela from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No bars, no raised fist, no grey-haired elder statesman. Keep the top left corner pale quarry wall.
heldForGuides.check: The 27 years, the release in 1990, the election of 1994 and the lime quarry were confirmed. The search did not return that the 1952 campaign followed Gandhi's method.

heldForGuides.fact: Born Temüjin, he was left fatherless and hunted as a boy. In 1206 he joined the warring peoples of the steppe into one nation, and his riders went on to build the largest land empire in history, tied together by relays of mounted messengers.
heldForGuides.art: Temüjin in the spring of 1206 by the Onon River in Mongolia, at the great gathering where he is named Genghis Khan: a tall, strongly built man in his forties with a broad forehead, a long beard and watchful, cat-like eyes, as a Persian writer who spoke to those who had seen him described him, in a plain belted robe of blue wool that crosses over the chest, felt boots and a fur-edged cap, his hair in a braid behind each ear. He stands on a spread of white felt before a tall pole from which hang nine white horse tails, the standard of the new nation, and looks out over our heads. In front of him, at the bottom of the picture, the chiefs of the steppe peoples have taken off their caps and hung their belts around their necks, and are kneeling. Round felt tents and horse herds stretch to the hills. Seen from among the chiefs, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No portrait of him from life exists: no horned helmet, no fur barbarian costume, no throne. Keep the top left corner open sky.

merge: Relics and Deeds: engine.js names each Relic and Deed by its key ('compass', 'press', 'antikythera', 'eureka', 'caravan', 'decree', 'eclipse', 'encore', 'fairwinds', 'ambush', 'trojan', 'rift', 'phalanx'). Every new Relic and Deed here has `as`: the existing card whose effect, cost and rules text it takes. To play them, the engine (and the EV handlers in ui.js that name those keys) must look up `CARDS[key].as || key` where it now compares the key. Two Relics with the same `as` do the same thing, so a player should not be able to have both in play (hasRelic should compare `as`). The engine has three Relic effects, so the 20 Relics here are seven that work as the Compass, nine as the Printing Press and four as the Antikythera Mechanism.
Relics have no faction in the game (f is 'N'), and that is kept, so any deck can play any of them. Deeds have a faction, and there are six in each of the five.

Mailed to Freedom takes the Trojan Horse's effect. If the Trojan Horse has left cards.js by the time of the merge, the engine has to keep that effect under this card's key (or another name) for the card to work.

Eras: cards.js has six eras and the last, The Age of Steam, ends in 1900. Eight Figures here have a year after 1900 (Einstein, Turing, Martin Luther King Jr., Jim Thorpe, Jesse Owens, Frida Kahlo, Houdini and Amelia Earhart), and so do the Wright Flyer and nine Deeds (Christmas Truce, Salt March, Penicillin, The Rite of Spring, The Lincoln Memorial Concert, Bridge of Spies, The Summit of Everest, Tutankhamun's Tomb Opened and Lascaux Found). The Figures are given era 6, the only value cards.js knows, and the Library would file them under 1800 to 1900. A seventh era is needed before they go in, for example { n: 'The Modern Age', to: 2000 }.

tx is written from k, arr and insp with the wording existing cards use; boldKeys and GLOSS in ui.js need no change. `links` goes into LINKS in text.js as it stands, `say` into SAY. No card here has a focus setting (FY): that is set when each picture is checked on the card.
Pronunciations (say) are given only where a reader might stumble, as in text.js.

Picture briefs: the 50 Relics and Deeds follow the notes of 2026-11-11 (the thing itself large, a few particular people at most, no rows of copies, both top corners plain). The 100 Figures' briefs were written before those notes: each keeps its top left corner clear but does not yet ask for the top right corner or for the head a fifth of the way down, and a few show more people than the notes allow. They need that pass before art is made.

Balance: node scripts/anoria/sim-set-150.js 12000 plays robot games with the new Figures added in memory and compares each with the Figures its faction already has. The Relics and Deeds cannot be played until the engine reads `as`; each is exactly as strong as the card it copies, but 50 more of them in the pool has not been tested.
